chapters.title: Interconnected Surface Water
chapters.scope_note: Kaweah’s three GSAs each filed a separate GSP under one Coordination Agreement. Kaweah’s ISW content sits with East Kaweah (EKGSA) and Greater Kaweah (GKGSA); Mid-Kaweah (MKGSA) reports no interconnected surface water and operates no ISW network (MKGSA GSP §4.7, p. 4-66 [PDF 244]). Colusa’s two GSAs (CGA and GGA) share one GSP. Yolo has a single GSA (YSGA).

sections.title: Model Type and Sophistication
sections.literature: There are three main methods of tracking and quantification ISW with models — analytical, numerical, and statistical (Zipper et al. 2022). While “numerical models are currently the gold standard for streamflow depletion estimation” they are less feasible in resource constrained settings (Zipper et al., 2022, Conclusions, p. 305). Analytical models are best for “rapid, screening-level assessments,” but less powerful with questions around attribution and mitigation (Zipper et al., 2022, Conclusions, p. 305). Statistical approaches cannot (yet) establish the causation SGMA compliance requires (Zipper et al., 2022, Methods, p. 288).

merced.text: MSGSA/MIUGSA/TIWD GSA-1 run MercedWRM, a quasi-3D numerical model built on the IWFM 2015 platform, calibrated against ET, groundwater levels, and streamflow (GSP §2.3.2, p. 2-207 [PDF 298]). Inputs include a county well-depth database of over 5,000 records and USGS CVHM texture data, which maps the coarseness and fineness of underground sediment (Appendix D §3.1.5, p. 3-3 [PDF 736]). Outputs are stream-aquifer flows by reach, neighboring subbasin, month, and water-year type. Depletion is the difference between a run with pumping and a run without it (GSP Table 2-11 through 2-14, p. 2-195 [PDF 286]).

east-turlock.text: ETSGSA/WTSGSA run C2VSimTM, the same model class (quasi-3D finite element, IWFM 2015) as Merced, calibrated October 1991–September 2015 against ET, groundwater levels, and streamflow (GSP §5.1.2, p. 5-3 [PDF 278]). Outputs include net stream-aquifer flux by river for historical, current and projected water budgets. This is the gain or loss from all causes, not pumping alone. The model also classifies each river node as gaining or losing (GSP §4.3.7, p. 4-50 [PDF 200]; GSP Table 5-7, p. 5-14 [PDF 289]). The GSP text calls these net figures ‘streamflow depletion, which is a different quantity from the paired-simulation depletion used for Merced (GSP §4.3.7, p. 4-50 [PDF 200]).

salinas-valley.text: SVBGSA runs SVIHM, a USGS-owned numerical model built on MODFLOW-OWHM v2. Outputs include a pumping attributable depletion estimate for the mapped interconnected stream segments coming from on model run with pumping and one without (Amendment 1 §5.6.2, PDF p191; Table 5-7, PDF p192) and mapped ISW locations. But the compliance criterion runs on shallow-well elevation readings, not on model output.

kaweah.text: The three GSAs share the Kaweah Subbasin Groundwater Flow Model, a MODFLOW-OWHM V2 model calibrated to groundwater elevations only (Modeling Report §2, GKGSA GSP [PDF 2473]). A streamflow routing package was added in 2023–2024 for potential future use. The GSAs state the model is not yet calibrated to estimate ISW depletion (ISW TM §1, GKGSA GSP [PDF 2742]). Depletion is instead estimated with an analytical stream-depletion function (Hunt 1999, 2005), run over a range of streambed and aquifer properties (ISW TM §3.2 [PDF 2761]).

colusa.text: The GSAs run C2VSimFG-Colusa, a numerical model adapted from DWR’s C2VSimFG, on a monthly timestep (GSP Appendix 3G [PDF 2455]). Outputs are simulated stream gains and losses for six reaches on the Sacramento River, Stony Creek and the Colusa Basin Drain. The model’s authors describe it as not yet well calibrated and label its ISW conclusions provisional (Appendix 3G [PDF 2455]).

yolo.text: YSGA runs a linked WEAP and MODFLOW model built from an earlier Yolo County IWFM (GSP §2.3.1, p. 2-149 [PDF 245]). Inputs include PRISM, CIMIS, LandIQ and eWRIMS data on a monthly timestep for WY 1971–2018. Outputs include simulated stream seepage by reach (GSP Table 2-18, p. 2-131 [PDF 227]).

sections.comparison: All six basins run a numerical model, and none uses model output directly as its ISW compliance measure. Kaweah, Colusa and Yolo each state that model uncertainty is the reason. Kaweah is the one basin that adds an analytical depletion function to fill that gap (see §1.2 and §1.8).

sections.title: Undesirable Result Threshold
sections.literature: The reviewed literature focuses on depletion-estimation methodology rather than the regulatory threshold-setting SGMA requires.

merced.text: Merced has not set an ISW-specific minimum threshold, measurable objective, or undesirable-result trigger. ISW criteria are carried over from the chronic-lowering-of-groundwater-levels indicator (GSP §3.8.2, p. 3-41 [PDF 400]). No depletion volume, streamflow rate, or stage value is used as a threshold in the Merced SMC.

east-turlock.text: East Turlock sets an ISW-specific undesirable result for each river. An undesirable result occurs on a river when 50% of its representative monitoring wells fall below their minimum threshold in two consecutive Fall events (GSP Table 6-20, p. 6-76 [PDF 450]). The thresholds are groundwater elevations, not flow or depletion values. The Merced River threshold is the Spring 2014 groundwater elevations, set with Merced ID (Table 6-21, p. 6-77 [PDF 451]; §6.8.2.3.1, p. 6-81 [PDF 455]). The Tuolumne and San Joaquin thresholds are the Fall 2015 low elevation (Table 6-21). The GSP treats these levels as a proxy for streamflow depletion (§6.8.2, p. 6-77 [PDF 451])

salinas-valley.text: The threshold approach changed between plan versions. The 2020 GSP set a volumetric minimum threshold at the current average depletion rate of 69,700 AF/yr (2020 GSP §8.11.2, GSP p. 8-58 [PDF 312]). Amendment 1 replaced it with a proxy: shallow groundwater elevations 1 foot above those observed in 2015 near mapped ISW locations (Amendment 1 §8.11.2, p. 8-61 [PDF 325]; §8.11.2.2, p. 8-64 [PDF 328]). The GSP determines the proxy from a hydraulic-gradient argument in EDF (2018) (§8.11.2.1.1, p. 8-62 [PDF 326]). It chose 2015 because it judged that surface water depletion then was not unreasonable (§8.11.2.1, p. 8-64 [PDF 328]).The reviewed text gives no rationale for the 1-foot margin. The undesirable-result test now triggers when any one shallow well falls below its minimum threshold (Amendment 1 §8.11.4.1, p. 8-68 [PDF 332]). During the evaluation period the ISW network had one usable well. The WY 2025 Annual Report reports two representative monitoring sites (RMS) wells in the network. The formal Sustainable Management Criteria table lists a threshold for one of them, and a threshold for the second, repaired well has not yet been set (WY 2025 Annual Report, Table 4-9, AR p. 102 [AR PDF 109]).

kaweah.text: The ISW technical memorandum (TM) calls its criteria “placeholder” SMCs and expects to revise them within one to two years (ISW TM §1, GKGSA GSP [PDF 2742–2743]). The GSAs state they cannot yet define a basin-wide quantitative undesirable result. The one numeric threshold covers one reach of the Lower Kaweah River: depletion that would push low flows below WY 2022 levels (ISW TM §3.3.1 [PDF 2764]). The ISW TM proposes setting measurable objectives and interim milestones equal to the minimum threshold, and will evaluate them once basin-wide thresholds exist (ISW TM §3.4 [PDF 2766]). It gives three reasons for doing so 1) data gaps and the lack of refined modeling tools, 2) a highly managed flow system, and 3) preliminary analyses showing limited depletion impact on channel losses. It will evaluate them once basin-wide thresholds exist. The ISW TM is Appendix 3D of the Greater Kaweah GSP, and GSP Section 5.9 presents the same preliminary criteria (GKGSA GSP §5.1, p. 5-2 [PDF 249]; §5.9, p. 5-87 [PDF 335]; §5.9.3, p. 5-102 [PDF 350]). The WY 2025 Annual Report calls ISW a data gap and reports two new shallow wells, but it gives no ISW criteria results (AR §5.6, p. 5-15 [PDF 48]).

colusa.text: An undesirable result occurs when the same three of twelve near-stream wells stay below their minimum thresholds for 24 consecutive months (GSP §5.3.6.3, p. 5-27 [PDF 355]). Eleven of the twelve minimum thresholds are the Fall 2015 depth to water plus 10 feet, which places each 10 feet deeper than the 2015 level (GSP §5.4.6.1, p. 5-50 [PDF 378]; Table 5-5, p. 5-53 [PDF 381]). The twelfth, at well 21N02W36A002, uses a deeper October 20, 2015, reading with no added 10 feet (p. 5-54 [PDF 382]). The GSP states that the 10 feet provides a margin of operational flexibility and was determined through discussion with the GSAs and stakeholders (p. 5-51 [PDF 379]). The Technical Advisory Committee record identifies the Fall 2015 level as the option consistent with EDF (2018). It selected the level 10 feet deeper because of concerns about constrained groundwater operations (Appendix 5B, p. 6 [PDF 2663]). Measurable objectives are the average of each well’s most recent five years of water levels (§5.4.6.2, p. 5-55 [PDF 383]). Interim milestones equal the measurable objectives (Table 5-5, p. 5-53 [PDF 381]). The criteria do not reference the reach-level depletion volumes in Appendix 3G.

yolo.text: Minimum thresholds are groundwater elevations at 17 near-stream wells in five ISW Management Zones, with a different method in each zone (GSP §3.8.2.1 [PDF 302–304]). An undesirable result requires exceedance at more than half the wells in two or more zones in the same year (GSP §3.8.1, p. 3-23 [PDF 301]). A single zone in exceedance becomes a watch area. The Upper Sacramento River threshold combines each well’s historic minimum elevation with 20 percent of its historic range (GSP §3.8.2.1.3, p. 3-26 [PDF 304]). The GSP describes it as set lower than historical conditions, to allow for expected cuts in surface water deliveries. Tables 3-4 and 3-5 set the thresholds about 63 to 65 feet below the measurable objectives at these three wells (pp. 3-27 to 3-28 [PDF 305–306]). The GSA states it intends to manage toward the objectives.

sections.comparison: Five basins set ISW criteria on groundwater elevations, and Kaweah sets a flow-based criterion on one reach. Most anchor thresholds to a recent drought: Fall 2015 in East Turlock and Colusa, WY 2022 in Kaweah, and period-of-record lows in most Yolo zones. No basin currently sets a threshold directly on a depletion volume. Salinas Valley’s 2020 volumetric threshold was replaced in Amendment 1.

sections.title: Volumetric ISW Depletion Estimates
sections.literature: Estimating volumetric streamflow depletion from observation data alone is generally not possible, because pumping effects are masked by other drivers of streamflow (Zipper et al., 2022). The standard calculation instead runs the model with and without pumping and takes the difference in stream-aquifer flux.

merced.label: Model: MercedWRM
merced.text: . The difference between the with-pumping and without-pumping runs (WY 1994-2023), averaged over WY 2018-2023, is 504,400 AFY of ISW depletion. The without-pumping run sets all urban and agricultural pumping in the subbasin to zero and keeps land use unchanged (GSP §2.2.7, p. 2-193 [PDF 284]). Pumping also raises inflow from, or lowers outflow to, neighboring subbasins by 141,800 AFY, which the GSP accounts separately (GSP §2.2.7, p. 2-194–195 [PDF 285–286]). The GSP does not use the 504,400 AFY figure to set any threshold or objective (GSP §3.8.2, p. 3-41 [PDF 400]). Instead, it uses groundwater levels as a proxy for the ISW indicator. It follows the DWR approach of showing that groundwater-level thresholds prevent significant and unreasonable ISW depletion (§3.8.1, pp. 3-39 to 3-40 [PDF 398–399]). The GSP treats historical depletion as not significant and unreasonable, then asks how much more would occur at the minimum thresholds. A 2020 hypothetical scenario with 8% more evapotranspiration was used to select groundwater levels that would constitute an undesirable result. It added 38,000 AFY of ISW depletion above the historical simulation, about 1.6% of average annual surface water outflow (p. 3-40 [PDF 399]). The GSP judges this increase small enough that the groundwater-level thresholds protect against ISW undesirable results.

east-turlock.label: Model C2VSimTM
east-turlock.text: East Turlock reports net stream-aquifer exchange for each river, not a depletion estimate. The model classifies stream nodes as gaining or losing and totals the exchange by river each year. WY 2025 results were a net gain of 40 AF on the Tuolumne River and 28,700 AF on the San Joaquin River. The Merced River had a net loss of 43,900 AF (Annual Report Table 8-6, p. 8-22 [PDF 65]). These totals come from the simulated flows alone, with no with-pumping and without-pumping comparison, so none is attributed to pumping. The GSP nonetheless calls these net values streamflow depletions, even where they show a net gain (GSP §4.3.7, p. 4-50 [PDF 200]). The Annual Report says planned model updates will allow scenario analyses that more clearly isolate the effect of subbasin pumping on streamflow depletion (p. 8-22 [PDF 65]). For compliance, the GSP uses groundwater elevations at monitoring wells against a fixed minimum threshold for each river (§1.2).

salinas-valley.label: Model SVIHM
salinas-valley.text: The 2020 GSP set a volumetric threshold at the projected average surface water depletion rate of 69,700 AF/yr (2020 GSP §8.11.2, p. 8-58 [PDF 312]). The GSP said it could not tell how much of that depletion was due to pumping without a no-pumping comparison (p. 8-58 [PDF 312]). The figure equals the average of the model’s net stream exchange term (Appendix 6B, PDF 586), so it reflects net stream-aquifer exchange, not pumping alone. First, a purely volumetric threshold 69,700 AF/yr (2020 GSP) was calculated as total surface-water depletion from all causes, which the GSP itself said could not be attributed to pumping specifically. Amendment 1 then ran the no-pumping comparison and produced a pumping-attributable ISW depletion figure of 8,400 AF/yr. This number was seasonally split into 2,600 AF/yr during peak conservation-release season (June–September) and 5,800 AF/yr non-peak (Amendment 1 Table 5-7, PDF p192). Amendment 1 replaced the volumetric criterion with a groundwater-elevation proxy, noting it was “unrealistic that the SVIHM will be updated annually” (Periodic Evaluation §2.7.1, PDF p78).

kaweah.label: Model: Hunt analytical function
kaweah.text: . One figure is published: 1.4 cfs of ISW depletion on the Lower Kaweah at People’s Ditch, averaged over the six lowest-flow months of WY 2022 (ISW TM Table 3-2, GKGSA GSP [PDF 2764]). The equation ran 100,000 times (Monte Carlo) with plausible ranges for each well distance from stream, aquifer property and streambed property. It is calculated as 5% of modeled pumping within a 2.5-mile corridor. The 5% is the upper end of the analytical model’s 2–5% range, applied because well locations are unknown (ISW TM §3.2 [PDF 2761]). The range applies to a six-month pumping period, so the figure covers near-term depletion only. The TM says the analytical model is unsuitable for long-term depletion, which awaits the refined groundwater model (p. 21 [PDF 2761]). A comparison of channel losses against pumping found little to no correlation (ISW TM §3.2 [PDF 2760]).

colusa.label: Model: C2VSimFG-Colusa
colusa.text: . The GSP body reports net stream gain, not a depletion volume. For WY 1990-2015 it gives net gain by stream and water-year type (GSP §3.2.7.1, Tables 3-6 and 3-7, pp. 3-80 to 3-81 [PDF 250–251]). It states that model uncertainty is too great to quantify stream depletion rates and volumes reliably (§5.3.6.2, pp. 5-26 to 5-27 [PDF 354–355]). The GSP’s scenario analysis is Appendix 3G, a July 2021 technical memorandum carried into the 2024 revised GSP unchanged (cover [PDF 2452]). The model sums stream gains and losses by reach each month. It does this for three 50-year scenarios (2016-2065): baseline future conditions, the baseline with 2070 climate change, and climate change with recharge projects (Appendix 3G, pp. 4–5 [PDF 2457–2458]). The Technical Memorandum (TM) refers to stream losses as depletions (p. 2 [PDF 2455]). It reports no pumping-only figure. The closest comparison is the climate scenario minus the baseline, in which Sacramento River net gains falls by 25,200 AF/yr, from 33,900 to 8,700 (Table 2, p. 18 [PDF 2471]). The TM attributes the change to added pumping for irrigation. The climate scenario also changes precipitation, evapotranspiration, and surface water supplies, so the difference is not a pumping-only estimate (p. 9 [PDF 2462]; p. 5 [PDF 2458]). The WY 2025 Annual Report does not report a depletion volume.

yolo.label: Model: WEAP/MODFLOW
yolo.text: . The GSP section on the quantity and timing of depletion presents simulated average seepage by stream reach, month and year (GSP §2.2.6.2.5, Table 2-18, pp. 2-129 to 2-131 [PDF 225, 227]). These are modeled exchanges between streams and groundwater, not pumping-attributable depletion. For example, the table shows 37,000 AF/yr lost from Lower Cache Creek and 30,000 AF/yr gained along the Yolo Bypass. The model is calibrated on Putah and Cache creeks and the Yolo Bypass area, and other streams are uncalibrated with significant uncertainty (p. 2-129 [PDF 225]). The GSP says the YSGA cannot directly measure depletion caused by groundwater use, and that model uncertainty makes thresholds based on model outputs inappropriate (GSP §3.8, p. 3-22 [PDF 300]).

sections.comparison: Merced, Salinas Valley and Kaweah report pumping-attributable estimates, by paired simulation or analytical function. East Turlock, Colusa, and Yolo report modeled stream-aquifer exchange, and their documents call it depletion. In five basins, the compliance test uses groundwater elevations. Kaweah’s flow threshold depends on a depletion estimate its model cannot yet provide.

sections.title: Measurement and Estimation Methods
sections.literature: Zipper et al. (2022) distinguish direct field measurement at the scale of an individual stream reach from regional model-based estimation (Zipper et al., 2022, Methods, p. 288). Barlow & Leake (2012) describe how direct field measurement works in practice, including transect-based approaches (Barlow & Leake, 2012, Results/Discussion, p. 23). Zipper et al. (2026) add a timing to model-based estimation. Depletion effects can lag behind pumping and only show up once a stream rewets in fall or winter. Building that delay into depletion models improved their match to observed streamflow (Zipper et al., 2026).

merced.text: ISW depletion estimates are model-based. The reviewed documents do not describe direct field measurement of stream-aquifer exchange. Physical monitoring is limited to 16 stream gages operated by other agencies (DWR, USGS, MID, USACE), none operated by a Merced GSA (GSP Table 4-10, p. 4-47 [PDF 447]).

east-turlock.text: Stream-aquifer exchange is estimated with the model. The reviewed documents do not describe streambed seepage measurement or GSA-operated stream gauging. The GSP acknowledges the ideal method — shallow wells transitioning away from the river — is not in use along the Tuolumne and Merced rivers (GSP §6.8.1, p. 6-74 [PDF 448]).

salinas-valley.text: The GSP designates shallow groundwater levels as the primary tool for assessing ISW depletion, measured at wells near the Salinas River (Amendment 1 §7.7, p. 7-25 [PDF 259]). Two existing wells from the Monterey County Water Resources Agency (MCWRA), 115 and 295 feet deep, were chosen using the preliminary SVIHM’s ISW locations, well depth, proximity to the river and nearness to a stream gage or River Series site. Two new wells are planned (§7.7.2, p. 7-27). The GSP bases this approach on EDF (2018) (§8.11.2.1.1, p. 8-62 [PDF 326]). Separately, SVBGSA’s documents include direct field measurement of stream-aquifer exchange. A 2026 Balance Hydrologics study of the Somavia Reach used five methods: synoptic-flow surveys, streamflow gaging, shallow piezometer clusters, riverbed temperature profiling and ring-infiltrometer measurements (ISW Report Executive Summary, PDF p7). The surveys and gaging measured flow loss by sub-reach, 10 to 16 cfs per river mile in the highest-loss sub-reach (Conclusions, PDF p30). Piezometers measured vertical head gradients, and the temperature and infiltrometer methods estimated infiltration (PDF p7).

kaweah.text: The GSAs use four approaches, each for a different purpose (ISW TM §2.3, §3.2 [PDF 2749–2761]). Spring 2017 and Fall 2022 depth to water, mapped with a 50-foot threshold following TNC’s ICONS method, identifies areas where ISW may be present (pp. 9–11 [PDF 2749–2751]). A gage-based channel-loss balance for the McKay Point to People’s Ditch reach (WY 2013-2022) is compared with pumping and groundwater levels. It showed little to no correlation, which the TM reads as depletion being a small part of channel loss (pp. 20–21 [PDF 2760–2761]). The Hunt analytical function gives a near-term depletion estimate for that reach (p. 21 [PDF 2761]). Landsat NDVI screening through TNC’s GDE Pulse, checked against aerial imagery, assesses historical effects on vegetation. Declines flagged at two sites traced largely to mining and vegetation removal (pp. 18–19 [PDF 2758–2759]). The TM says the causal link between pumping, depletion and flow is best assessed with and without pumping model runs, which await the refined groundwater model (p. 17 [PDF 2757]).

colusa.text: Measurement combines the model with 12 near-stream wells read each spring and fall (GSP §4.2.5.4, p. 4-37 [PDF 326]). Wells are under 200 feet deep and between 2,000 feet and five miles from a stream. The GSP cites EDF (2018) for the proxy and for excluding wells within a few thousand feet of a stream. The Technical Advisory Committee record says the criteria were developed using EDF’s recommendations (Appendix 5B, pp. 5–6 [PDF 2662–2663]). EDF (2018) does not state the depth of five-mile limits. The 15 stream gages are state and federal installations and describe flow rather than compute depletion (GSP §4.2.4.3, p. 4-32 [PDF 321]).

yolo.text: Groundwater levels at 17 shallow near-stream wells serve as the proxy, measured each spring and fall (GSP §3.8, p. 3-22 [PDF 300]). The GSP cites EDF (2018) for the rationale, the gradient principle and a target of one well every 4 to 6 miles along a stream (GSP §4.8.2, p. 4-21 [PDF 327]; §4.8.4, p. 4-27 [PDF 333]). Other well criteria, such as depths under 220 feet preferred an historical variation above 10 feet, are listed separately (p. 4-22 [PDF 328]). Stream gage data is compiled each year but is not linked to the SMC (GSP §4.8.2, p. 4-22 [PDF 328]).

sections.comparison: All six rely on model estimates and groundwater-level or flow proxies, and Salinas Valley has also commissioned direct field measurement. Kaweah adds remote-sensed vegetation screening checked against aerial imagery. Three basins cite EDF (2018) for the groundwater-level proxoy: Salinas Valley, Colusa, and Yolo. Kaweah uses TNC methods and datasets.
sections.gaps: The Salinas Valley field study's own stated limitation was that it focused on the river-to-shallow-sediment connection and did not examine connectivity to the 180-ft aquifer, which is where the pumping happens (ISW Report §5, PDF p32).

sections.title: Per-well Attribution and the Cumulative Pumping Problem
sections.literature: The cumulative pumping problem refers to the fact that the total impact from multiple wells may not equal the sum of their individual effects (Zipper et al., 2018). Some tools exist to address it. Fienen et al. (2017) rank individual wells by their impact on streamflow to target reductions and Zipper et al. (2018, 2019) develop methods to attribute depletion to specific wells, though these methods tend to underestimate depletion.

merced.text: The documents do not describe per-well or per-parcel attribution. Private agricultural pumping is spread evenly across model grid cells, so the model cannot resolve individual wells. With the paired all-pumping-off simulation the model does not capture the cumulative-pumping math problem since everything is turned off and on at once. GSP does not mention the cumulative pumping problem. The only spatial breakdown is by receiving water body and by neighboring subbasin. Depletion is attributed to where it lands rather than to a source well.

east-turlock.text: Attribution is also at river scale. The GSA acknowledges that groundwater elevations used as a proxy can't isolate the effects of its own pumping from pumping in neighboring subbasins along the same shared boundary rivers (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.1.4.1, p. 8-18 [AR PDF 61]). The GSAs' response is to coordinate across the Modesto Subbasin boundary on baseline years to use for thresholds rather than mathematically separating the two basins’ contributions.

salinas-valley.text: The documents do not describe per-well attribution. As the compliance criterion is one well’s elevation reading and not a modeled output, it cannot distinguish between drop in water level due to pumping and drop because of a dry year (reservoir operations). In WY 2022 the single-well threshold was reached. On review, the cause was determined to be due to lack of summer releases from the upstream reservoir, not because pumping increased (Periodic Evaluation §2.7.2, PDF p79). The documents do not describe a method for separating a pumping effect from causes outside GSA control.

kaweah.text: Attribution is aggregate: all pumping within a 2.5-mile buffer of the reach, multiplied by a flat 5% (ISW TM Table 3-2 [PDF 2764]). The GSAs note that well locations and depths near potential ISW are largely unknown (ISW TM §2.4 [PDF 2751]). The voluntary Well Registration Program is named as the way to fill this input (ISW TM §3.2 [PDF 2761]). The ISW TM does not discuss the cumulative pumping problem.

colusa.text: Depletion is attributed by reach, summed across model elements along each reach (Appendix 3G [PDF 2457]). The GSP names the cumulative problem directly. Wells deeper than 200 feet or farther than five miles are excluded from the ISW network. The stated reason is that their capture from multiple sources cannot be resolved with existing data and models (GSP §5.3.6.3, p. 5-27 [PDF 355]).

yolo.text: Depletion is assessed at the scale of an ISW Management Zone, and the documents do not describe per-well attribution. The GSP uses attribution language for subsidence and salinity but not for ISW. DWR’s corrective action 4e asks YSGA to identify the users affected by pumping-induced depletion (WY 2025 Annual Report [AR PDF 17]).

sections.comparison: No basin attributes depletion below the reach or zone scale, and none applies the literature’s per-well tools. Colusa and East Turlock name the problem in their own documents. Kaweah names the missing input, well locations, and ties it to a voluntary registration program.
sections.gaps: Attribution matters because pumping impacts differ widely among wells. Well-level estimates let managers target reductions where they matter most and spread responsibility among pumpers (Fiene et al., 2017). The literature has developed initial tools to attribute depletion to individual wells. None of the six basins’ documents describes applying, testing, or citing them. All six work at basin, reach or zone scale, which the literature treats as a starting point. Kaweah and Yolo identify missing well location or screen-depth records as a limiting input.

sections.title: Aquifer Depths
sections.literature: Pumping depth matters for ISW depletion because stream-aquifer flow has a vertical component that a water level at one depth may not show. Regional models are often calibrated to laterally distributed water levels, which constrain vertical flow poorly (Pasner et al., 2026). In the Sacramento Valley, three models reproduced observed heads comparably but simulated different surface water–groundwater exchanges (Pasner et al., 2026). Where a well is screened below a semi-confining layer, leakage through that layer can supply part of the pumped water. Ignoring it can overestimate the share taken from the stream (Butler et al., 2007). A low-permeability layer does not remove the connection. Depletion can still occur over the long term through leakage across it (Malama et al., 2021). Pumping responses in such layers can be small and delayed (Malama et al., 2021). A basin’s existing well network may therefore miss depletion that a well at a different depth would have caught. Pasner et al. (2026) use 81 continuously monitored well nests to measure vertical gradients that lateral water-level data do not capture.

merced.text: Aquifer-depth handling is assumption-based. Well perforation data is largely unavailable, so the vertical distribution of pumping is assigned using an assumed depth range from a county database (Appendix D §3.1.5, p. 3-3 [PDF 736]). Separately, the July 2026 Rules tie allocation eligibility and well-construction approval on pumping from above the Corcoran Clay in subsiding zones (Rules §2.2.3.2, p. 26 [PDF 28]; §3.2.10, pp. 56–57 [PDF 58–59]). The policy is aimed at subsidence control. It may shift pumping toward the shallow aquifer, where the GSP’s maps place most interconnected reaches.

east-turlock.text: The ISW monitoring network is confined to the shallower aquifers, on the reasoning that only shallow systems connect to rivers — but within that network, wells are screened hundreds of feet below the water table (GSP §7.1.6.2, p. 7-11 [PDF 476]). During WY 2025 the GSAs installed three vertically nested well clusters specifically to close this gap and see how conditions differ by depth at a single spot (Annual Report §8.1.4, pp. 8-16–17 [AR PDF 59–60]). However, Sustainable Management Criteria have yet to be set for these new wells.

salinas-valley.text: The interconnected shallow sediments sit above the Salinas Valley Aquitard, while essentially all pumping happens below it, in the 180-Foot principal aquifer (Amendment 1 §5.6.2, PDF p191). The 2026 field studies measured the river-to-shallow-sediment link but explicitly did not examine connectivity to the 180-ft aquifer (ISW Report §5, PDF p32). The link between the pumped aquifer and the river has not yet been measured. DWR's own Recommended Corrective Action 2 asked the GSA to investigate hydraulic connectivity between the shallow zone and the principal aquifers (Periodic Evaluation §1.1.2, PDF p21).

kaweah.text: The model divides the aquifer at the Corcoran Clay into Upper and Lower Aquifers, informed by an airborne electromagnetic survey (Modeling Report §2 [PDF 2472]). Most SMC are set separately for each. The ISW network uses Upper Aquifer wells only (EKGSA GSP §4.7.3.1 [PDF 301]). Subsidence is attributed mainly to the Lower Aquifer, which sits outside the ISW analysis (Modeling Report §3.6 [PDF 2486]). Well screen intervals are listed as a significant data gap (Coordination Agreement App. 5 [PDF 440]).

colusa.text: The ISW network admits only wells screened shallower than 200 feet, so deeper pumping sits outside the indicator (GSP §5.3.6.3 [PDF 355]). The GSP notes that nested wells can show vertical gradients (GSP Table 4-1 [PDF 294]). A planned model refinement would adjust layer thicknesses to better distribute pumping by depth, with no date attached (Appendix 3G [PDF 2470]).

yolo.text: Wells shallower than 220 feet were preferred for the ISW network, with the deepest at 350 feet (GSP §4.8.2, p. 4-22 [PDF 328]). The shallow and intermediate zones are treated as connected because no confining layer has been observed. The model documentation notes that screening depths are often missing, which made it hard to tell which layer a well pumps (Appendix E §3.3 [PDF 88]).

sections.comparison: Five basins monitor ISW with shallow wells. They handle deeper pumping differently: by exclusion (Colusa), by an assumed connection (Yolo), or by stating the link as unmeasured (Salinas Valley, Kaweah). East Turlock has added nested wells. Missing screen-depth records limit depth analysis in Merced, Kaweah and Yolo.

sections.title: Limitations in Scope, Monitoring, Funding
sections.literature: The reviewed literature doesn't address monitoring-network funding or institutional capacity directly. Its focus is on modeling and measurement methodology, not on how GSAs build or sustain the infrastructure those methods depend on.

merced.text: Monitoring gaps are self-acknowledged, including a lack of spatial density guidance for ISW networks (GSP §4.10.3, p. 4-47 [PDF 447]). The GSP states that the ISW depletion understanding could be improved with additional groundwater elevation data near some streams and rivers (GSP §4.10.6, p. 4-48 [PDF 448]). DWR’s own best practice guidance does not provide specific spatial density standards for ISW monitoring networks, so Merced has no external benchmark to work from (GSP §4.10.3, p. 4-47 [PDF 447]). The GSP also records repeated requests to the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation for river restoration monitoring data that have not been answered (GSP §4.10.7, p. 4-48 [PDF 448]).

east-turlock.text: Monitoring gaps are disclosed and being addressed. The fix is funded through a DWR technical-support grant rather than the GSAs' own recurring revenue (Annual Report §8.1.4, pp. 8-16–17 [AR PDF 59–60]). A comprehensive well re-survey also found elevation errors significant enough to have produced a false undesirable-result exceedance (Annual Report §8.2.3, p. 8-31 [AR PDF 74]).

salinas-valley.text: For the entire evaluation period, the ISW monitoring network consisted of one usable well, after a second was found to be screened beneath the aquitard and removed (Periodic Evaluation §2.7.2, PDF p79). The replacement well was installed through a competitive DWR grant, the Sustainable Groundwater Management Round 1 Implementation Grant (Periodic Evaluation §1.2.2, PDF p30). The WY 2025 Annual Report is the first document to report data from the updated network. It confirms the replacement well is now reporting groundwater elevations. Its threshold has not yet been set, so Sustainable Management Criteria coverage remains one well while data collection has expanded to two (WY 2025 Annual Report §4.2.6.1, Table 4-9, AR p. 102 [AR PDF 109]).

kaweah.text: The ISW TM lists nine data gaps, including shallow wells, stream gages and well-specific pumping data (ISW TM §4.3 [PDF 2772]). The criterion runs on three shallow wells plus gages, and many network sites are proposed rather than built (ISW TM §4.2.1 [PDF 2770]). New wells and gages depend on grant funding (EKGSA GSP §6.7.7 [PDF 499]). Two new shallow wells came online in WY 2025 (Annual Report §5.6.2 [PDF 48]). The GSAs also note that the fully appropriated Kaweah River has no minimum flow or flow objective (ISW TM §1 [PDF 2742]).

colusa.text: The GSP states that existing gages cannot measure depletion and that model uncertainty is too great for reliable quantification (GSP §5.3.6.2 [PDF 354–355]). Stony Creek has no active gage below Black Butte Lake, and Colusa Drain outflow is not monitored (GSP §4.2.4.4 [PDF 321]). Remedies are listed as GSP Studies, including a westside streams program costed at $225,000 for the first year (GSP §7.1.2.4 [PDF 516]). None carries a completion date.

yolo.text: The model is calibrated for Putah and Cache creeks and the Yolo Bypass only (GSP §2.2.6.2.5 [PDF 225]). Ephemeral streams in the Dunnigan Hills are named as a data gap (GSP §4.8.5 [PDF 333]). Related monitoring projects list cost and funding as TBD (GSP Appendix J). DWR’s corrective action 4 asks YSGA to revise its ISW SMC. YSGA plans to respond by the 2027 Periodic Evaluation, with 2032 as a fallback (WY 2025 Annual Report [AR PDF 17]).

sections.comparison: Every basin states its monitoring gaps openly. New ISW wells and gages are mostly grant-funded (East Turlock, Salinas Valley, Kaweah), and Colusa and Yolo list remedies without dates or funding sources yet. In Kaweah, the accounting platform runs on fees while the ISW network depends on grants.

sections.title: Gaps and Uncertainty
sections.literature: The literature reviewed flags the importance of both turning modeled output into actionable management decisions and regulatory planning but does not necessarily lay out an approach for doing so within SGMA (Morrisett et al. 2024; Zipper et al., 2019; Zipper et al., 2022; Zipper et al., 2026). This chapter calls that step closing the loop — a monitored or modeled value triggers a defined management response. Along with the lack of completeness in the compliance loop, uncertainty is rarely communicated to water managers alongside depletion estimates (Zipper et al., 2022).

merced.text: The loop closes on the groundwater-level proxy rather than on any ISW depletion quantity. Meaning a management response follows when monitored groundwater levels cross a trigger level, not when an ISW depletion volume exceeds a limit. The July 2026 Rules build an automatic allocation-adjustment mechanism triggered by groundwater levels, with an explicit numeric uncertainty buffer. But the uncertainty buffer links to the level trigger, not to any depletion figure. The reviewed documents do not attach error bounds or confidence intervals to either depletion figure.

east-turlock.text: The loop closes on an ISW-specific criterion. An undesirable result was declared on two of three rivers in WY 2025 (Annual Report §8.1.4.1, p. 8-17 [AR PDF 60]), but produced no management consequence because Interim Milestones were pre-set below the Minimum Thresholds. The GSP set 2027 Interim Milestones below the Minimum Thresholds because long-term declines led the GSAs to expect levels to fall below thresholds while projects were being developed. The Annual Report reads this result against those milestones, and all seven wells with milestones stayed above them. The milestones rise to the thresholds in 2032, when projects are expected to support recovery (Annual Report §8.1.4.1, p. 8-17 [AR PDF 60]; GSP §6.3.3, p. 6-23; §6.2.6, pp. 6-5–6-6). The GSAs acknowledge the criterion can't attribute the condition to their own pumping. ISW-specific numbers are reported without confidence intervals.

salinas-valley.text: The loop also closes on the proxy: an undesirable result was declared for WY 2022, but the GSA attributes it to reservoir operations rather than pumping (Periodic Evaluation §2.7.2, PDF p79), and no consequence or management action followed. The WY 2025 Annual Report applies the same criterion and finds no exceedance and no undesirable result (WY 2025 Annual Report §4.2.6.3, AR p. 103 [AR PDF 110]). But elsewhere in that same report, a year-over-year decline at one well is described as something that "could indicate that due to pumping, more depletion of ISW occurred in WY 2025 than in WY 2024" (WY 2025 Annual Report, AR p. 61 [AR PDF 68]). In WY 2022 a decline on the same proxy was attributed to reservoir operations. The report does not state a method for telling the two causes apart.

kaweah.text: Uncertainty is reported in three ways. The model publishes calibration statistics, including an RMSE of 32.2 feet (Modeling Report Table 15 [PDF 2539]). The analytical depletion estimate carries a 90% likelihood range, and the ISW designations have their own uncertainty section (ISW TM §2.4, §3.2 [PDF 2751, 2761]). The WY 2025 Annual Report reports ISW work plan progress rather than a compliance test (Annual Report §5.6 [PDF 48]). GKGSA’s rulebook counts streambed percolation within the Native Sustainable Yield it allocates (GKGSA R&R §3.02(a)(A) [PDF 12]).

colusa.text: Uncertainty is described in prose, and ISW conclusions are labelled provisional. Groundwater-level calibration statistics are published, with 92% of observations within ±25 feet (Appendix 3D §5 [PDF 2416]). Appendix 3G notes that simulated Sacramento River net gains are smaller than the ±2.5% accuracy of gage measurements (Appendix 3G [PDF 2469]). No ISW-specific action is tied to an exceedance. In WY 2025 no well exceeded its minimum threshold (WY 2025 Annual Report §6.1.5, AR p. 46 [AR PDF 52]).

yolo.text: Uncertainty is described in prose in the model appendix, which names stream–aquifer interaction as an area of large uncertainty (Appendix E §3.3 [PDF 88]). YSGA states that model uncertainty makes model-based thresholds inappropriate (GSP §3.8, p. 3-22 [PDF 300]). No well exceeded its threshold in WY 2025 (WY 2025 Annual Report §4.5 [AR PDF 45]). A draft tiered well-permit review asks whether a proposed large well may affect nearby ISW, and Yolo County makes the final decision (YSGA Tiered Well Permit Review Process, draft 2024).

sections.comparison: In all six basins, compliance runs on a groundwater-level or flow proxy rather than a depletion quantity. Kaweah attaches a likelihood range to its depletion estimate, and no other basin bounds a depletion figure. The stream–aquifer interface enters binding instruments in two places: Yolo’s draft well-permit screen and GKGSA’s allocation of streambed percolation.
sections.gaps: This is the literature’s stated gap as it appears in practice. No basin turns model output into a management decision through an ISW quantity. Kaweah is the one basin to state a numeric likelihood for a depletion estimate.

chapters.title: Land Repurposing
chapters.scope_note: The Merced findings in this chapter are MSGSA’s. In the Turlock Subbasin the program is East Turlock’s (ETSGSA); West Turlock has no land repurposing program, though the grant was awarded to the Subbasin as a whole. In Salinas Valley the MLRP grant is held outside the GSA. In Kaweah the grant is held at subbasin level and implemented by the three GSAs. Colusa and Yolo hold no MLRP grant and appear only in §2.10.

sections.title: Financing
sections.literature: The reviewed literature does not address how repurposing programs are financed or which entity holds the grant. Its MLRP papers are siting and scenario tools built independently of any funding arrangement (Nuñez-Bolaño et al., 2025; Dybala et al., 2025).

merced.text: Two funding streams. The local one is a Proposition 218 fee funding the Phase 1 Land Repurposing Program, launched in WY 2022 as voluntary three-to-five-year incentive agreements. The state one is a Department of Conservation MLRP block grant of $8.89 million, awarded 16 June 2023 and held by MSGSA directly (GSP §6.2.2, p. 6-8 [PDF 469]). The grant funds five implementation projects under contract and a $750,000 development solicitation (planning, design and permitting only) that opened in October 2025. Grant activities must be complete by March 2027.

east-turlock.text: ETSGSA applied “on behalf of both GSAs” and “DOC awarded the Subbasin a grant of $8.89 million”, with a work plan that “focuses primarily in ETSGSA, but will have applicability across the Subbasin” (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.2.5, pp. 8-34 to 8-35 [AR PDF 77–78]). The grant is therefore subbasin-wide and the program is East Turlock's. The grant closes 31 March 2027.

salinas-valley.text: The grant is larger and the GSA does not hold it. The Greater Monterey County Integrated Regional Water Management (IRWM) Group was awarded a $10 million grant by the California Department of Conservation through MLRP. IRWM is partnering with SVBGSA, the Central Coast Wetlands Group, the California Marine Sanctuary Foundation and the Resource Conservation District of Monterey County for development and implementation (Response to DWR, PDF p56). The money covers the 180/400, Eastside and Langley subbasins, and it buys land rather than paying for practices.

kaweah.text: The Kaweah Subbasin received $10 million in MLRP funding, according to a Self-Help Enterprises comment reproduced in the GSPs (EKGSA GSP comment matrix [PDF 1941]). The GSP bodies do not describe the program. The WY 2025 Annual Report lists three recharge basin projects receiving MLRP funding, two by GKGSA member ditch companies and one by EKGSA (Annual Report §4.3 [PDF 31]). Stated targets are about 238 acres converted to recharge basins and 65+ acres restored for habitat and community or tribal use (EKGSA GSP comment matrix [PDF 1942]).

sections.comparison: All four grants come from the Department of Conservation and range from $8.89 to $10 million. The grantee is a GSA in Merced and a regional non-GSA group in Salinas Valley. In East Turlock and Kaweah the subbasin holds the grant, run by one GSA and three GSAs respectively. Where grantee and SGMA entity differ, program results need a separate route into the accounting.

sections.title: Verification Triggers
sections.literature: The standard method of evapotranspiration minus effective precipitation across the growing season tested against metered pumping, found it works well on actively irrigated fields. However, it degrades on partially irrigated and mixed-use parcels, and cannot be applied directly to fallowed or transitioning land, because negative precipitation deficits are masked to zero **(**Zipper et al., 2024). Anderson et al. (2018) add that restored wetland uses roughly as much water as an irrigated field at first, and only saves water as the vegetation matures. Ultimately the parcels a repurposing program creates are exactly the parcels the standard ET method handles worst. The review's broader gap statement is that no paper it covers documents a post-implementation verification approach for MLRP water savings at all.

merced.text: Repurposed parcels are measured quarterly, the same way they do for regulatory compliance. Consumptive use is “the annual value of Evapotranspiration (ET) as determined by the default remote sensing source in the GAP, currently OpenET, minus the annual Effective Precipitation value” (Rules §2.5.2.3, p. 34 [PDF 36]), and the Phase 1 repurposing agreements are monitored on that same data. Quarterly OpenET monitoring showed “water use reductions for some participants is coming in lower than expected, due to trees remaining in the ground and soil moisture retention from the especially wet WY 2023” (Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-9 [PDF 54]). Fallowing itself is verified separately and only for the absence of irrigation, using aerial imagery, spatial data, or site inspections, but not for the magnitude of water savings (Rules §2.5.2.1.5, p. 33 [PDF 35]).

east-turlock.text: ET tracking is turned off on MLRP land. Parcels and fields related to its MLRP, IFP, and other programs will not be subject to the measurement and reporting Consumptive Use (ET) and Effective Precipitation, or the calculation of Consumed Groundwater Use (Rules and Regulations Phase 2, §4.04, pp. 14–15 [PDF 14–15]). The same section applies a quantified three-stage remote-sensing test to landowners who fallow on their own initiative without payment. Cumulative ET minus effective precipitation at or below 0.5 acre-feet per acre is checked first, failing that July ET at or below 0.1 acre-feet per acre, failing that a visual check of aerial imagery. Unpaid fallowing is measured against numeric thresholds, and paid repurposing parcels are exempt from ET measurement.

salinas-valley.text: The documents on disk do not describe a verification protocol for land repurposing. The one activity with a measured water result is arundo eradication, measured by a field study of vegetation types rather than by tracking parcels (§2.4).

kaweah.text: All three GSAs track consumptive use parcel by parcel with satellite ET, and this is the binding compliance basis. MKGSA adopted Land IQ ET because GSA-wide metering could not be put in place in time (MKGSA GSP §6.7.1.2, p. 6-53 [PDF 390]). EKGSA’s rulebook defines ET as measured with satellite imagery and ground-based truthing (EKGSA R&R §1.11 [PDF 2]). Under GKGSA’s rules, verified fallowed land is not debited for consumptive use. The rule does not state how verification is done (GKGSA R&R §4.03(e) [PDF 17]).

sections.comparison: Three basins hold a parcel-scale ET instrument and apply it to repurposed land differently. Merced measures enrolled parcels, East Turlock exempts them, and Kaweah stops debiting verified fallow land without a written verification test. Merced is the one basin that currently produces a measured water figure tied to a specific repurposing agreement.
sections.gaps: The literature says the ET-minus-precipitation method is least reliable on transitioning land, and no basin describes testing that reliability on its own repurposed parcels. No grantee basin runs a paired comparison of expected against measured savings on an enrolled parcel, which is the check the literature's verification gap describes.

sections.title: Allocation and Leakage
sections.literature: Additionality (proving real additional benefits beyond a baseline) and leakage (production or pumping moving elsewhere) are identified as preconditions for crediting co-benefits (Bryant et al., 2020). The main questions raised are whether the water savings would not have happened without the identified intervention and whether the entitlement to pump moves after the pumping stops.

merced.text: Landowners are not required to give up their groundwater allocation when they enroll in MLRP. The application asks: "Will the landowner give up any groundwater allocation under the scope of the project proposed?" (MLRP Development Project Application, p. 6 [PDF 14]). Most keep it, and the binding Rule allows that kept allocation to move. Allocation is based on a parcel's total acreage, not how much of it is irrigated, so idled land keeps earning its full allocation. Since idled land isn't debited for water use either, the allocation accumulates. It can be carried over to future years or transferred to another parcel nearby, and the Rule does not require a copy of the transfer agreement to be filed (§2.4.4.1.2). One mechanism in the same Rule does stop water attached to a non-agricultural land use from becoming tradeable, which is the Managed Wetland Water Allocation. This sets a qualifying pre-existing wetland's allocation at its historical use, restricts that water to habitat maintenance, and recalculates the allocation if the habitat isn't sustained. It applies to existing wetlands rather than to repurposed land, and measures water delivered and acreage held rather than habitat condition.

east-turlock.text: Forfeiture is part of what the payment buys. Fields fallowed on the landowner's own initiative keep their allocation; fields enrolled in the MLRP or the Incentivized Fallowing Program have it “rescinded for the period specified in the Project Agreement”; cover-cropped fields keep it and receive an effective-precipitation credit (Rules and Regulations Phase 2, Article V, p. 26 [PDF 26]). Two qualifiers travel with this. First, the rescission is temporary and tied to the agreement term — it is not permanent. Second, the mechanism that would let a retained allocation move has not been adopted: "Transfer" is defined as "[to be determined]" in both rule versions, carryover is confined to the account that generated it and expires after three years, and pooling may not cross a Priority Action Area boundary. The trigger is payment rather than repurposing, so a landowner cannot be paid for not pumping and also keep the entitlement to pump, for as long as the payment lasts.

salinas-valley.text: The question does not yet arise, because no allocation system is in place. Amendment 1 revised the fallowing and land-retirement management action so that it “could be undertaken with or without pumping allocations” (Table 3-1, PDF p92). Allocations remain a future work item, named among four priorities for FY2027. The program acquires the land or takes a long-term lease, so the pumper is removed rather than regulated.

kaweah.text: Fallowing removes the consumptive-use debit and leaves the allocation in place (GKGSA R&R §4.03(e) [PDF 17]). Allocations can be carried over and transferred, including between GSAs within the subbasin (EKGSA R&R §3.01(e)(3) [PDF 6]). GKGSA’s transfer leave-behind rises with distance, from 20% to 70% for Tier 1 and 40% to 90% for Tier 2 (GKGSA R&R §4.03(c) [PDF 16]). From WY 2025 the zonal leave-behind no longer applies to Native Sustainable Yield credits (GKGSA R&R [PDF 14]). Two pilot market auctions ran in 2024 on the Water Dashboard (MKGSA GSP §6.7.3.1 [PDF 394]).

sections.comparison: A repurposed parcel’s entitlement is either retained and portable (Merced, Kaweah) or suspended for the paid term (East Turlock). Salinas Valley removes the pumper by acquisition. Kaweah is the one basin that scales its transfer leave-behind by distance, and the one with a trading market in operation.
sections.gaps: The literature asks for additionality and leakage to be settled before a co-benefit is credited. East Turlock addresses leakage by suspending the entitlement, and Kaweah through a distance-based leave-behind on transfers. No basin publishes the allocation status of repurposed parcels, so movement of freed entitlement is not reported.

sections.title: Water Savings from Land Repurposing
sections.literature: The literature introduces some clear approaches. One paper combines satellite energy-balance ET with LandIQ land use classification to produce a before-and-after water use matrix for thirty-six land use conversion pairs, with fallowing producing the largest savings and restored wetland consuming about as much as an irrigated field (Anderson et al., 2018). Zipper et al. (2024) quantify how closely the ET-minus-effective-precipitation method tracks metered pumping — a mean absolute error of 81 mm and a 4.9% bias at field scale, improving at management-area scale — and note that it rests on locally calibrated deep-percolation assumptions that most California GSAs do not have.

merced.text: Water savings are calculated as measured consumptive use, per parcel, through GAP. The approximate consumptive use reduction from land repurposing in WY 2025 was 4,655 AF (Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-9 [PDF 54]). The five-year goal is 25,911 AF, roughly 5,200 acre-feet a year, so the WY 2025 shortfall is on the order of ten percent. Quarterly ET monitoring detected a shortfall and named its physical causes (residual orchard trees still transpiring).

east-turlock.text: Water savings are estimated once, before implementation, using satellite ET data, estimated at 2.7 acre-feet per acre of consumptive use and not compared against measured use afterward. Three months after the initial 2024 estimate, GSP Appendix K redid the same six-practice analysis using the basin groundwater model instead and got a different number, 2.9 acre-feet per acre. That is one of four different published totals for MLRP demand reduction across the documents; none should be treated as a re-check of another. There are two more qualifiers of importance. First, the suitability study located enough land for only 17,000 of the 21,000 acre goal. The gap is filled by a placeholder, "Miscellaneous Repurposing," worth 11,700 acre-feet of water savings (nearly a fifth of the largest published total). If that acreage is delivered through land retirement, it would carry no co-benefit requirement. Second, East Turlock measured a 25,000 acre-foot reduction in WY 2025 from cover cropping and voluntary fallowing rather than the MLRP. The MLRP itself had a handful of approved pilot projects and none built yet.

salinas-valley.text: The adopted management action states a benefit type with no quantity. Fallowing, the fallow bank and land retirement are dependent on program participation with a stated benefit of decreased groundwater extraction for irrigated agriculture (Periodic Evaluation Table 3-2, PDF p113). The one land-use-change activity with a measured water figure is arundo (an invasive grass) eradication, which is run outside the GSA's own program. The document publishes a per-acre conversion factor (reduction in consumptive use of 21.1) with error bounds (+/- 3.0) based on the average difference in ET between untreated arundo and herbaceous vegetation (Periodic Evaluation §3.3.1, PDF p96). But the savings are from both groundwater and surface water sources, and they're reported across the whole Salinas River corridor rather than for the 180/400 Subbasin specifically. The subbasin accounting does not currently use this figure.

kaweah.text: The documents do not attach a water-savings target or figure to the MLRP, whose published targets are in acres. For fallowing generally, savings are implicit in the ledger. GKGSA stops debiting verified fallow land (GKGSA R&R §4.03(e) [PDF 17]). EKGSA credits back ET measured on fallowed land above effective precipitation (EKGSA R&R §1.09–1.10 [PDF 1]). EKGSA’s Flying Dragon project cites a 1,000 AF recharge design yield (EKGSA Stakeholder Engagement Report [PDF 8]).

sections.comparison: Two designs appear. Merced, East Turlock and Salinas Valley produce a savings number, and they differ in timing: after implementation, before implementation, and from measured replacement vegetation. Kaweah records fallowing only as a missing debit in a per-parcel ledger. That needs no separate measurement and produces no program-level total.
sections.gaps: The literature reports its own accuracy numerically (Zipper et al.'s 81 mm mean absolute error and 4.9% bias, Anderson et al.'s validation against eight flux towers). No basin attaches an uncertainty range to a land-repurposing water figure, with a single exception: the Salinas Valley arundo study publishes plus-or-minus bounds on every value. But those bounds are unlabeled as the source does not say whether they are a standard deviation, a standard error or a confidence interval.

sections.title: Data Source and ET Product Choice
sections.literature: The range of water savings estimates is based as much on the selection of land use layers and crop identification (Anderson et al., 2018) as much as the ET data product selected for measurement (Zipper et al., 2024), with neither typically being locally validated.

merced.text: OpenET, delivered through the Groundwater Accounting Platform, is used both for quarterly monitoring of repurposing agreements and for parcel-level consumptive use under the Rule. Two alternatives to the default are allowed (1) another commercial remote-sensing source which requires an annual attestation and quarterly ET reporting, and (2) flow meters that convert metered pumping to consumptive use through a published Efficiency Factor table crossing irrigation system type with SAGBI-derived soil drainage. A landowner who doesn't keep up alternative's reporting duty defaults to OpenET, and anyone who combines methods across parcels is checked against remote sensing. However, OpenET was available only through 2021 at the time of the model update, so CIMIS reference evapotranspiration was used to extend it, and “the CIMIS station was decommissioned by DWR in early 2024” (Annual Report [PDF 60]).

east-turlock.text: LandIQ is the data product GSA-wide (GSP §8.1.2.1, p. 8-30 [PDF 524]) with CalETa used for the 2012–2021 historical baseline. The land use layer is DWR's 2020 Crop Layer. With the ET product there is a complete published conversion-factor layer showing irrigation efficiency for fourteen methods, from 60% to 95%, cited to UC ANR Publication 8570, plus several other cited factors covering effective precipitation, water-year determination, cover-crop standards and extraction-to-consumption conversion.

salinas-valley.text: SVBGSA’s land-repurposing accounting does not use an ET platform. The one ET-based figure comes from a field study of two vegetation types, covered in §2.4 (Zefferman and Barker 2024).

kaweah.text: Land IQ supplies field-level ET for MKGSA, calibrated with ground sensors (MKGSA GSP §6.7.1.2 [PDF 390]). GKGSA’s rules name Land IQ datasets for identifying irrigated parcels (GKGSA R&R §4.03(b) [PDF 13]). EKGSA’s rulebook defines ET as satellite-measured with ground truthing and does not name a vendor. The documents do not publish the ground-truthing stations or a validation comparison.

sections.comparison: Three ET products are in use (OpenET, LandIQ with CalETa, and Land IQ), and each serves as the consumptive-use basis for parcel accounting. East Turlock and Merced publish their conversion factors. No basin documents a local validation of its ET product against field measurement, which both literature papers treat as the precondition for trusting the number.

sections.title: Benefits Considered Beyond Water Savings
sections.literature: Quantifying benefits of land repurposing is well documented in the literature, but benefits are quantified individually and are hardly operationalized. There are approaches to show how groundwater-dependent ecosystem services (pollinator habitat, pollution remediation and carbon stock) can be quantified by spatial overlay from public GIS data (Howard et al., 2023). Thresholds exist to determine the groundwater level at which vegetation shows adverse impact, roughly 4 metres statewide (Rohde et al., 2024). An open-source framework scores agricultural livelihoods, water quality, climate resilience and biodiversity from land cover class and area alone, with uncertainty attached to the result (Dybala et al., 2025). On the community side, recharge benefit can be attributed to specific communities by combining recharge suitability, domestic well capture zones and a vulnerability index (Marwaha et al., 2021); groundwater levels can be converted into counts of domestic well failures prevented (Pauloo et al., 2020); and water, nitrogen and economic effects of retiring land can be quantified within and around disadvantaged communities (Fernandez-Bou et al., 2022).

merced.text: Co-benefits are scored at application rather than measured. The MLRP application allocates weighted points: 35 for water quality and supply, 25 for disadvantaged community benefits, 25 for agricultural and economic resiliency, and 25 for regional ecological benefits. Further points awarded for geographic prioritization, feasibility and cost-effectiveness, a proposed wildlife corridor, regional coordination and other considerations. Each category is a set of checkboxes with a half-page narrative. The rubric does not state a formula, unit, or published scoring threshold. Ecological elements include habitat connectivity, species of interest, groundwater dependent ecosystem benefits, floodplain reconnection, and a residual “Other Ecological Benefits: Other benefits not quantified above”. The application does include one spatial component: a half-mile buffer around disadvantaged communities and a one-mile buffer around small water systems, layered with residential well density. This helps identify where a project may have the greatest potential for benefits to disadvantaged communities and socially disadvantaged farmers and ranchers (Application Appendix B, p. 21 [PDF 29]). Measurability is itself a scored attribute, appears only in the water category, and is optional. The criterion asks for benefits “which can be measured or noted consistently,” with a footnote reading “If you are able to describe methods of measurement or observation, please add that information into this category's narrative.”

east-turlock.text: Only the groundwater benefit is required. The 2026 application asks applicants to describe habitat benefits, benefits to disadvantaged communities, benefits to the local economy and other benefits each marked “if applicable” (§2.3.2, p. 8 [PDF 8]). While they don’t carry metrics, they are priced. The published Type 1 rate schedule starts at $730 per acre per year for fallowing only, $890 for extended fallowing, $1,050 for recharge basins, $1,300 for rewilding and $1,590 for floodplain reconnection. Extended fallowing and rewilding carry the identical water obligation (crop removal and irrigation cessation for at least 10 years), so the $410 difference is the price of the habitat obligation. The rates are based on cost built from NRCS EQIP comparables, member-agency implementation experience, industry equipment and labor rates, and a balance against the Groundwater Use Fee. No acre-foot, habitat unit or species count underlies any rate. On the community side, there is no distance criterion, mapping requirement, or scoring input. The one quantified, citable community-facing standard — a 400-metre buffer drawn from published research (Fernandez-Bou et al. 2023) — was applied to schools rather than disadvantaged communities, and is not carried into the operative 2026 program.

salinas-valley.text: There is an ecological quantification here, but not directly tied to MLRP. Following Rohde et al. (2024), the 2026 groundwater-dependent ecosystem report computes a threshold for each mapped ecosystem. It flags an ecosystem as of concern in a given year when its greenness falls more than one standard deviation below its own historical average and depth to groundwater is below that threshold. Thresholds are computed only where the relationship between greenness and depth is statistically significant and negative. The workflow runs in R from Landsat imagery and county groundwater elevations, so it can be repeated annually at low cost, and it produced a year-by-year result: potential ecosystems of concern in 2015, 2021, 2022 and 2023, and none in 2019, 2020 or 2024. Field condition is separately scored at fourteen sites using the California Rapid Assessment Method. However, there are a few caveats. First the method is being considered and not adopted. Second, it is not yet tied to a sustainable management criterion. Third, it measures the consequence of groundwater depth rather than the consequence of repurposing. Applying it to repurposing would mean running it on repurposed parcels against a counterfactual. On the community side, a siting consideration for water quality and access to drinking water wells is applied. The benefits named for the MLRP itself are stated in the conditional, without metrics.

kaweah.text: Habitat and drinking-water benefits for disadvantaged communities are named, in the conditional, for two MKGSA recharge projects (MKGSA GSP §6.6.17.1, §6.6.18.1 [PDF 381, 383]). Flying Dragon, a 58-acre EKGSA project near Seville, names 1,000 AF of recharge, habitat, a walking trail and a conservation easement (EKGSA Stakeholder Engagement Report [PDF 8]). The documents do not describe scoring, pricing or measurement of co-benefits.

sections.comparison: Every grantee basin names ecological, community and economic benefits, and none measures an outcome for them inside its repurposing program. Merced scores benefits at application and East Turlock prices them by practice. Salinas Valley holds an unadopted ecological method, and Kaweah’s one described project uses a conservation easement. Kaweah’s MLRP is the one to name a tribal beneficiary.
sections.gaps: The literature supplies methods for exactly the benefits these programs claim and cannot measure — spatial overlay for ecosystem services, per-polygon vegetation thresholds, per-hectare multi-benefit scoring, capture-zone attribution of recharge benefit to communities, and well-failure counts derived from groundwater levels. The literature does not yet link these quantifications to a crediting system. One of those methods is in use in one basin (Salinas), by a non-GSA partner, and is unadopted. None of the basins describes a standardized community health or equity measurement protocol. No GSA in the six basins applies CalEnviroScreen, and no environmental health index is applied to a repurposing decision.

sections.title: Monitoring Protocol
sections.literature: The reviewed MLRP papers are prospective mainly. Tools built for siting and prioritization tend to leave a gap between which parcels to target and whether targeted parcels (Nuñez-Bolaño et al., 2025). Scenario-based frameworks describe projected outcomes rather than verifying delivered ones (Dybala et al., 2025). There is a lack of research that documents a post-implementation verification approach for MLRP water savings or co-benefits. The closest thing to a monitoring method in the set is a threshold that can be recomputed each year from data already being collected (Rohde et al., 2024).

merced.text: Monitoring is split by benefit type. Water is monitored quarterly and post-implementation through OpenET, as described in §2.2. Projects must deliver at least ten years of benefit, and a matching monitoring obligation has not yet been set. A Merced-specific monitoring plan is not yet publicly available.

east-turlock.text: The monitoring architecture spans several documents. A draft Project Implementation Monitoring Plan sets phases, frequencies, roles, quality assurance and grant reporting. Additionally, five practice-specific Implementation Standards each add their own monitoring section. Two activities are always required: a photo log and a conditions description. The quantitative items are optional and conditional on seeking a surface water or recharge credit. For Consumed Surface Water Credits, monitoring of pumped water diversion for irrigation is needed and for Recharge Credits, a staff gauge and a camera trap that records daily pictures of water levels in the pond during the rainy season (Implementation Standards, Stormwater Ponds, Monitoring [PDF 8]). Ecological monitoring is a fixed annual form based on cover estimates for treated area (visual: <25%, 25–50%, 50–75%, >75%). Dominant species presence, notes on target natives vs. invasives, and survival estimate for installed plants (visual percent) is required. No threshold attaches to any value, and the assessment is a yes-or-no line on the project checklist. Structurally, the landowner is the monitor and the agency verifies completeness of the monitoring information submitted (i.e., forms photos), and confirms GPS/time stamps and consistency with photo-points. Results are aggregated for reporting to the Department of Conservation. So, the protocol answers whether the project was built and persists, annually for ten years, with georeferenced evidence. It does not enter the groundwater ledger and does not answer how much benefit it produced, for any category including water.

salinas-valley.text: A monitoring protocol for land repurposing is not yet in place. The subbasin is working on its Multi-benefit Agricultural Land Repurposing Plan as well as a regional monitoring plan.

kaweah.text: Water use is monitored continuously through the allocation ledger. Land IQ ET is tracked per parcel per month and shown to landowners on the Water Dashboard (MKGSA GSP §6.7.1.1–6.7.1.2 [PDF 389–390]). The documents do not describe monitoring for habitat, recreation or community benefits. MKGSA uses Sustainable Conservation’s Groundwater Recharge Assessment Tool (GRAT) to find parcels for acquisition (MKGSA GSP §6.6.11.1 [PDF 370]).

sections.comparison: Water monitoring on repurposed land comes from the allocation ledger in Merced and Kaweah rather than from a program-specific protocol. East Turlock’s program protocol records whether a project was built and persists, not how much benefit it produces. Kaweah’s documents describe no co-benefit monitoring, and Merced and Salinas Valley are developing plans.
sections.gaps: Both the literature and the plans offer limited guidance on post-implementation monitoring. Monitoring plans are in development in Merced and Salinas Valley.

sections.title: Post-MLRP Funding
sections.literature: The review found literature mentioning the need for financial models for securing long-term funding for monitoring, maintenance and adaptive management after MLRP block grant expiration. Nothing in the reviewed papers proposes one.

merced.text: The documents do not describe a post-grant plan. The MLRP grant deadline for project activities is March 2027 (Annual Report [PDF 63]), and projects must deliver at least ten years of benefit, with a perpetuity option available. No document identifies a funding source for monitoring or maintaining those benefits after March 2027.

east-turlock.text: The grant closes 31 March 2027, obligations and monitoring run ten years, and record retention is 3 years after grant close or for any other period specified by the Project Incentive Agreement. A recurring Groundwater Use Fee exists, but no document connects fee revenue to post-grant monitoring. Type 1 payments are also made up front in one lump sum for the full 10-year implementation period.

salinas-valley.text: SVBGSA states the risk directly: “Ongoing funding requirements and reliance on grants pose a challenge for long-term implementation” (Periodic Evaluation §3.3.1, PDF p97). Salinas identifies the MLRP Plan to guide the program into subsequent years if there is community interest and funding.

kaweah.text: The documents do not describe post-grant funding for MLRP monitoring. The accounting platform runs on pumping fees. MKGSA’s Water Dashboard cost about $165,000 to develop, with about $10,000 a year for maintenance, paid from Emergency Ordinance fees (MKGSA GSP §6.7.2.4, p. 6-56 [PDF 393]). A $10 per AF administrative fee on all groundwater use funds administration (MKGSA GSP §6.7.1.1 [PDF 389]).

sections.comparison: No grantee basin has a financial model for co-benefit monitoring after the grant ends. Recurring fees fund water accounting in Merced and Kaweah, and Kaweah is the one basin that publishes what its accounting platform costs. Salinas Valley names grant reliance as a risk in its own documents.

sections.title: Dust
sections.literature: The review names dust emissions from fallowed and transitioning land as a serious potential harm (Fernández-Bou et al., 2025), but no real accounting system currently relates to per parcel land repurposing efforts.

merced.text: Mentioned, not measured. Dust is part of the stated reason the program exists. The RFP's background says that “When improperly managed, idle fields can emit dust and worsen air quality… Multibenefit Land Repurposing is a beneficial alternative that aims to reduce potential negative impacts.” (RFP pp. 2–3 [PDF 3–4]). Air quality then appears twice more as an unmeasured checkbox item in the community benefit criteria. No particulate metric, emissions factor, monitoring requirement, baseline or threshold appears in any Merced document.

east-turlock.text: Mentioned, not measured. Dust is treated as a landowner responsibility. The Implementation Standards require the landowner to maintain the land in a way that does not create harm due to dust emissions, among other impacts (Rewilding, Requirements/General, p. 2 [PDF 2]). Dust appears as a benefit in an optional best practice: a perimeter hedgerow that buffers wind. Additionally, the Vegetated Cover standard lists “Decreased particulate and other air emissions” among its objectives, but with no measurement method attached.

salinas-valley.text: Not mentioned. Word-boundary searches return zero hits for dust, PM10, particulate and air quality across the 2020 GSP, Amendment 1, the Periodic Evaluation, the Response to DWR, the ecosystem report and the WY 2025 Annual Report.

kaweah.text: Dust appears in survey boilerplate and in CEQA permitting text for recharge basins (e.g., MKGSA GSP §6.6.6.3 [PDF 362]). GKGSA’s fallowing rule requires parcels to be maintained to limit vegetation growth (GKGSA R&R §4.03(e) [PDF 17]). The same rulebook does not include a dust, air-quality or ground-cover provision.

sections.comparison: No basin has a field-scale dust accounting method. Two name dust as a repurposing issue without measuring it, in opposite roles: a harm repurposing prevents (Merced) and a nuisance the landowner must avoid (East Turlock). In Kaweah, an ET-based fallowing exemption is paired with a rule to keep fallowed land free of vegetation.
sections.gaps: The literature identifies the harm and does not supply a protocol. Two of the grantee basins identify the harm and do not describe a measurement. A dust accounting method would therefore need to be built rather than adopted from existing work. That makes it a candidate for a recommendation to DWR rather than a finding about any one basin.

sections.title: Other Repurposing Programs Beyond MLRP

merced.text: The locally funded Phase 1 Land Repurposing Program predates the block grant. It is funded through a Proposition 218 fee and uses three-to-five-year voluntary incentive agreements. As of WY 2025, 14,128 acres of land have been repurposed (Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-9 [PDF 54]). It is also the source of the measured water figure discussed in §2.4. Merced’s measured repurposing figure comes from the local program rather than the grant program. Two further land-status categories in the Rule function as repurposing. First an Inactive designation, which is annual and freely reversible, and second a permanent Riparian Area carrying a 150-foot average width standard along watercourses. Both keep earning allocation and neither is debited for evapotranspiration, as described in §2.3.

east-turlock.text: Two programs sit alongside MLRP. First the IFP, which requires a three-year commitment whereas the MLRP requires a ten-year commitment. The IFP also does not require multibenefit outcomes from fallowing, just demand reduction and avoidance of dust or weed growth on adjacent lands (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.2.5, p. 8-35 [AR PDF 78]). Running a non-multibenefit program next to a multibenefit one at a published price difference acts as a control case for the multibenefit premium. The second program is Land Retirement, positioned as the MLRP's backstop as deficits in MLRP acreage goals could be achieved through this program. It is faster to implement because it incentivizes growers to fallow or retire land without co-benefit requirements. Appendix K also records that its incentive design will consider reverse bids. Separately, cover cropping is by acreage the largest demand-reduction activity in the GSA, roughly 25,000 acres in WY 2025. It is accounted for inside the allocation rule through an effective-precipitation multiplier conditioned on a cited ground-cover standard.

salinas-valley.text: Voluntary fallowing, a fallow bank and agricultural land retirement are separate from the MLRP grant and are land-repurposing activities in the GSP. The fallow bank is a pooled fund that anybody fallowing land can draw against the bank to offset lost profit from fallowing (Periodic Evaluation Table 3-2, PDF p113). The documents do not specify how it is capitalized, who may draw on it, at what rate, or how draws are accounted for. Three further activities function as repurposing without carrying the label: arundo eradication along the river corridor (§2.4), the Salinas River Stream Maintenance Program's vegetation and sediment management, and floodplain enhancement and recharge work.

kaweah.text: Several activities outside the MLRP repurpose or idle land. Tulare Irrigation District’s on-farm recharge program ran district-wide in 2023 (Modeling Report §3.5, GKGSA GSP [PDF 2470]). In MKGSA, measured recharge is converted to allocation with a 10–25% deduction and issued the following year (MKGSA GSP §6.7.1.1 [PDF 389]). The basin also took part in LandFlex, which paid growers to idle land where it would help protect household and small-system wells (EKGSA GSP comment matrix [PDF 1942]). The 21-acre Okieville Recharge Basin, next to a disadvantaged community, was built in 2024 (EKGSA GSP comment matrix [PDF 1941]).

colusa.text: Colusa holds no MLRP grant, and Appendix 7A notes that the program primarily targets critically overdrafted subbasins (GSP Appendix 7A [PDF 2895]). The main repurposing-type activity is The Nature Conservancy’s winter flooding of farmland for shorebird habitat and recharge.
