The program estimates about 5.2 taf/yr of net recharge, about 1.3 feet per participating acre, and the basin model gives a similar figure (GSP §6.3.3.9 [PDF 425]; Appendix 3G [PDF 2461]). Recharge is to be determined by mass balance, as in the 2018–2021 pilot (GSP §6.3.3.8 [PDF 424]). The Demand Management Program lists multi-benefit land repurposing, fallowing and dry farming as voluntary measures, without measurement or reporting (GSP §6.3.6.2 [PDF 439]). Monitoring is done by landowners, TNC and irrigation districts rather than the GSAs.

yolo.text: Yolo holds no MLRP grant, and YSGA does not run an incentive program. Repurposing-type projects sit in the GSP project list, and most have not started (GSP Appendix J). They include cover cropping and rangeland improvement, winter water retention on rice fields, and oak woodland and riparian restoration. Most are led by community groups, a Tribe, districts or the County, and some draw on NRCS EQIP, CalFire and Healthy Soils funds. A 2025 YCFC&WCD pilot recharged 150 AF on a 30-acre fallowed field over 45 days, measured with nearby wells (WY 2025 Annual Report [AR PDF 10]). About 31,000 acres of managed wetlands are being added to the YSGA model (GSP §4 [PDF 338]; WY 2025 Annual Report [AR PDF 10]).

sections.comparison: In every basin, the activity that repurposes or idles the most land sits outside the MLRP. Several of these activities enter the ledger: Merced’s Phase 1 program, East Turlock’s cover-crop credit, and MKGSA’s recharge-to-allocation cycle. In Colusa and Yolo, measured recharge on farmland is reported but not credited, and implementation rests mostly with non-GSA partners.

chapters.closing_note: A caveat on what these gaps mean per basin. The document sets are not equally complete. Several of the absences noted for Salinas Valley in this chapter are gaps in document availability, not demonstrated absences: an MLRP Plan, the multi-criteria siting tool's specification, and the demand management framework are not yet available. Merced and East Turlock each had a full set of program instruments to work from — an RFP and application, implementation standards, a monitoring plan, an incentive payment framework, and binding rules — while Salinas Valley had none of these. The one exception is the allocation finding in §2.3. East Turlock on the other hand is mainly architecture rather than results. No projects have been implemented as of the most recent document, the monitoring plan is a draft, and the program plan itself is unfinalized. So East Turlock's absences are weaker findings than the equivalent ones for Merced, which were tested against a rule that's in force. Kaweah’s MLRP program documents (grant agreement, program plan, scoring criteria and monitoring plan) are not on disk. Most of what is known about the program comes from a Self-Help Enterprises public comment and an EKGSA newsletter. Kaweah’s absences are therefore absences in the filed plans. MKGSA’s allocation provisions were read from the GSP’s description of its Emergency Ordinance. Colusa and Yolo appear only in §2.10. Yolo’s project table (Appendix J) has no text layer and was read by OCR.

chapters.title: Community Considerations
chapters.scope_note: Merced’s three GSAs share one GSP and differ on procedural access. The standing disadvantaged-community seat is MIUGSA’s (PE §8.1, p. 8-4 [PDF 133]) and the fee-gated appeals are MSGSA’s (MSGSA Rules and Regulations, July 2026, §5.1.1.2). TIWD GSA-1 has no instrument on disk. In the Turlock Subbasin the Rules, the fee, the accounting platform and the MLRP outreach contract are East Turlock’s. In Salinas Valley all community material reviewed is SVBGSA’s. Kaweah’s three GSAs file separate GSPs. The Mitigation Plan findings are MKGSA’s, the Community Management Area provisions are GKGSA’s and EKGSA’s, and the engagement metrics are EKGSA’s. Colusa’s two GSAs share one GSP, and the private pumper seat is CGA’s only. In Yolo, dry-well assistance and well permitting are Yolo County functions.

sections.title: Stakeholder Advisory Committee
sections.literature: While the literature does not touch on the specific Stakeholder Advisory Committee directly it does note the importance of equitable governance. Formal representation on a governing board has been shown to predict equitable plan content better than outreach activity does (Dobbin et al., 2023). Even with collaborative structures it appears that the smallest communities gain the least (Dobbin & Lubell, 2021). Also, a seat on the board is not necessarily sufficient on its own. While joint powers/multi-agency structures for GSAs do raise average DAC representation on boards, the smallest and least-incorporated communities don't benefit proportionately (Dobbin, 2020). Consultation becomes meaningful when there is real authority to shape a decision (Sorgen et al., 2025).

merced.text: The Stakeholder Advisory Committee is advisory and sits outside the decision chain, which runs from the Coordination Committee to the three GSA boards, and only becomes effective once each GSA board approves the Committee's recommendations (GSP §1.2.5.7.1, p. 1-57 [PDF 90]). MIUGSA separately operates a Stakeholder Guidance Committee with a standing seat for disadvantaged communities (PE §8.1, p. 8-4 [PDF 133]). That seat appears in the Periodic Evaluation and not in MIUGSA's own Rules, which assign the Committee no role, consultation right or equity-analysis requirement (MIUGSA Rules and Regulations, Oct 2023). The documents do not show the seat carrying formal authority. No Merced document records advisory input changing a rule or a threshold.

east-turlock.text: A Stakeholder Advisory Committee is not part of the 1,428-page GSP adopted in 2022 (full-text search). It was formed in spring 2025 and has met three times, including one meeting held at a working farm (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.2.5, p. 8-35 [AR PDF 78]). Both GSA boards are member agencies only (GSP §3.3.1, pp. 3-19–3-20 [PDF 145–146]). The designated disadvantaged-community seat is a deliverable in Self-Help Enterprises' MLRP contract, on a Steering Committee (MLRP Outreach & Engagement Plan, p. 6 [OCR PDF 6]). The Steering Committee’s powers are not defined in the documents on disk, which include no charter or roster (MLRP Outreach and Engagement Plan; 2026 Application; Implementation Monitoring Plan; WY 2025 Annual Report).

salinas-valley.text: The eleven-member SVBGSA Board includes a voting director representing disadvantaged communities and public water systems. Castroville Community Services District appoints it (2020 GSP Appendix 11A, PDF p900). The position is defined in the Joint Powers Agreement (2020 GSP Appendix 2A, PDF p452). The Advisory Committee and the Subbasin Implementation Committee are advisory (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.1, PDF p178), and SVBGSA states that it has not established the standing disadvantaged-community body its own 2019 assessment recommended (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.8.1, PDF p183).

kaweah.text: GKGSA’s eleven-member board includes seats nominated by a Rural Communities Committee and a Stakeholder Committee, plus a California Water Service seat (GKGSA GSP §2.7.2, p. 2-27 [PDF 73]). The Rural Communities Committee is made up of local public agencies and a municipal wells representative. Decisions pass by simple majority. MKGSA’s Mitigation Plan Advisory Committee includes disadvantaged-community representatives and reviews whether claims qualify for funding before Board approval (MKGSA Mitigation Plan §3.2.4–3.2.5 [PDF 37]). A 2014 door-to-door survey by Self-Help Enterprises and CSU Fresno led GKGSA to classify Cameron Creek Colony as severely disadvantaged (GKGSA GSP §2.7.1, p. 2-22 [PDF 68]).

colusa.text: Each GSA board is the final decision-maker, and technical advisory committees advise them (GSP §2.7.2.1 [PDF 166]). CGA’s board includes two Private Pumper Representatives appointed through the county (GSP §1.3.1, p. 1-3 [PDF 115]). GGA’s nine seats are agency seats. The GSP’s engagement table gives disadvantaged communities an inform-and-involve purpose and tribes an inform, involve and consult purpose (GSP Table 2-8 [PDF 163]). The documents do not describe a designated disadvantaged-community seat.

yolo.text: YSGA is a joint powers authority, and the agencies serving its three designated disadvantaged communities hold voting board seats (GSP §1.5.2 [PDF 64]). These are California American Water, Knights Landing CSD and UC Davis. The Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation is a voting JPA member. In Dunnigan, some households rely on domestic wells rather than the member utility. In response to NGO comments, YSGA added a DAC map, tribal lands and a domestic well depth figure to the GSP (GSP comment matrix [PDF 466]).

sections.comparison: Designated seats take three forms: a community category (Salinas Valley, MIUGSA), agencies that serve communities (Yolo, GKGSA), and private pumpers (CGA). A seat’s durability follows the instrument that creates it, from a JPA to a contractor scope of work. Kaweah’s Mitigation Plan is the one case that places an advisory committee inside a funding decision.

sections.title: Meaningful Benefits
sections.literature: A community benefit counts as meaningful when it changes a household's material position, beyond just naming it in a plan. Delivered benefits fail when a community cannot afford to sustain them (Fernandez-Bou et al., 2021). Benefits become measurable when engagement runs ahead of siting and the community's priorities set the project the accounting is run on (Katrak-Adefowora et al., 2026).

merced.text: Community benefit is defined in the MLRP solicitation and not in the SGMA documents. The solicitation lists drinking water security, economic and workforce benefits, green space, recreation, air quality and educational opportunities (MLRP RFP, p. 6 [PDF 7]). These carry 25 application points as checkboxes, with no metric and no published scoring threshold (Application pp. 10–19; Disadvantaged Community Benefits category, p. 12 [PDF 18–20]). The GSP's project template has no disadvantaged-community benefit field.

east-turlock.text: GSP Chapter 8 requires a disadvantaged-community benefit statement for each of its 29 projects and management actions, with a separate field for a volumetric quantity (GSP Chapter 8, p. 8-10 [PDF 504]). Seven of the disadvantaged-community fields read “Benefits to disadvantaged communities overlap with the benefits described above for sustainability indicators” (GSP Chapter 8, p. 8-10 [PDF 504]). For the accounting platform the stated community benefit is exclusion of de minimis extractors — small domestic well users who pump below a certain threshold are exempt from certain measurement or reporting requirements (GSP §8.1.2.3.4, p. 8-40 [PDF 534]).

salinas-valley.text: For land retirement the plan states that participation is unknown, so benefits cannot be quantified in advance. Castroville Community Services District board identified, in its own words, the specific things its residents need to be informed about regarding sea water intrusion including that it would affect their health, water bills and home values (PE §7.4.8.2, PDF p183).

kaweah.text: The term is not used, and the GSP project templates do not include a disadvantaged-community benefit field. Community benefits appear at project level. Flying Dragon is sited near Seville, and the Okieville Recharge Basin has a stated drinking-water purpose (EKGSA Stakeholder Engagement Report [PDF 8]; EKGSA GSP comment matrix [PDF 1941]). Neither carries a measurement.

colusa.text: The term is not used. The multi-benefit recharge program lists community water supply first among its objectives. It then describes community benefits as potential and ancillary, depending on where projects are sited (GSP §6.3.3.1, pp. 6-34 to 6-35 [PDF 419–420]). Siting criteria are recharge suitability and shorebird habitat.

yolo.text: The term is not used. Appendix J carries a yes-or-no Disadvantaged Community column for each project. The documents do not define what the flag means or what follows from it (GSP Appendix J).

sections.comparison: Community benefit appears as a required field (East Turlock), a yes-or-no flag (Yolo), a stated objective (Colusa), a solicitation category (Merced), or a project purpose (Kaweah). None is paired with a unit of benefit. Across the six basins, the shared missing piece is the unit rather than a place to record it.
sections.gaps: The one specification of community benefit written by a community names health, water bills and property values with regards to seawater intrusion. The basin does not describe monitoring them and no reviewed paper offers a groundwater-accounting method for them either. This is a gap on both sides, not an unused method.

sections.title: Procedural, Distributional and Representative Equity
sections.literature: The three kinds of equity outlined here reinforce each other and are not direct substitutes (Koebele et al., 2023). Representative equity, fairness in who holds a seat and a vote, can be granted formally, but withheld in practice (Dobbin, 2020). Procedural equity, fairness in who can participate in the decision making process, have fixes that are cheap and specific: translation, childcare, transit and meeting timing (Fernandez-Bou et al., 2025). Distributional equity, fairness in who bears the outcomes and burdens a decision produces, was found to be the questions with the lowest barrier to answer but the ones getting the least attention (Perrone et al., 2023).

merced.text: Procedural equity with regards to who can appeal an enforcement action or land-use classification, on what timeline, and whether the GSA must explain itself varies between GSA in Merced. MSGSA's Rules give landowners a 30-day appeal and a variance from a pumping limit the Board must reason (MSGSA Rules §§5.1.1, 6.1.1.7, p. 70 [PDF 72]). Standing is limited to holders of a fee interest, and both routes are fee-gated with no hardship waiver (MSGSA Rules §§1.3.56, 1.3.58, 5.1.1.2, 6.1.1.2). MIUGSA charges no fee and extends standing to lessees, widening access on those two counts (MIUGSA Rules, Definitions, p. 1 [PDF 3]; §1.15). Its appeal window is ten calendar days, and variances pass on a two-thirds vote without stated reasons (MIUGSA Rules §6.8.a, §1.15.c). Neither GSA’s rule includes a language-access provision, one of the low-cost procedural measures the literature identifies (MSGSA and MIUGSA Rules, full-text search).

east-turlock.text: Procedural rules set fixed timelines without a requirement for Board explanation. An Owner or Operator, a term that includes lessees, can appeal an annual fee figure within 30 days of notification (Phase 2 §4.07, pp. 23–24 [PDF 23–24]). The General Manager then has 60 days to investigate. The Board has another 60 days to decide. Together that can take roughly five months. If the challenge relies on the Owner's own metering data, the Owner must supply it, since ETSGSA does not otherwise require it. A successful appeal carries a new obligation: the appellant's wells must then be registered with the Groundwater Accounting Platform. A second, general appeal route covers any other dispute over how the rules apply to a parcel or account (Phase 2 §8.01, p. 34 [PDF 34]). But the Board is only required to consider it, not to decide in the appellant's favor. Neither process charges a fee. Neither requires the Board to state its reasons.

salinas-valley.text: SVBGSA’s board pairs a designated seat with a supermajority rule. A disadvantaged-community director holds a seat, providing formal representation (2020 GSP Appendix 11A, PDF p900). Ordinary business passes on a majority of the eleven-member Board, but fees and pumping limits require a super majority: eight of the eleven Board members, including an affirmative vote by three of the four agricultural representatives (2020 GSP §2.2.1, p. 2-7 [PDF p51]). So, the disadvantaged-community, environmental and public directors cannot carry either decision over agricultural objection. No document records a failed vote, so this is architecture rather than cause. The supermajority rule is the point where formal representation and decision authority diverge.

kaweah.text: GKGSA’s rulebook lists Community Management Areas as “[To be determined]”, and the next section fully specifies a management area for dairies and processing plants (GKGSA R&R §4.04–4.05 [PDF 18]). EKGSA’s rules give its Board power to create community management areas (EKGSA R&R §3.02 [PDF 6]). MKGSA’s Mitigation Plan gives tenants interim drinking water regardless of well ownership (MKGSA Mitigation Plan §3.1 [PDF 30]). Technical-assistance claims are not eligible if the claimant’s pumping exceeds their native yield allocation (MKGSA Mitigation Plan §3.2.5 [PDF 37]).

colusa.text: Procedural access includes 242 meetings before October 2021, three public comment periods on each agenda, and paired daytime and evening sessions (GSP §2.7.2.1 [PDF 164–167]). On the distributional side, Appendix 5E counted domestic well impacts at candidate thresholds. The revised thresholds reduced projected impacts from 589 wells to 99 (Appendix 5E Table 1 [PDF 2711]). The documents do not describe a representative seat for drinking water users.

yolo.text: Representation runs through member-agency board seats (§3.1.1). Yolo has no allocation or fee system, so the documents contain no mechanism that distributes pumping limits or costs between groups. Procedural provisions are covered in §3.2.

sections.comparison: Representative and procedural equity vary independently. Salinas Valley pairs a board seat with a supermajority rule, and Colusa pairs extensive procedure with no designated community seat. Distributional provisions appear where allocations exist, as in Kaweah’s undefined Community Management Area. No basin reports which residents bear dewatering risk, though the literature calls this the most computable equity type.

sections.title: Domestic Well Protection as an Equity Outcome
sections.literature: Research reveals that most GSPs do not integrate stakeholders comprehensively, and domestic wells inside disadvantaged communities are significantly less protected than wells outside them (Perrone et al., 2023). Locally set thresholds are generally consistent with well health decline and a meaningful share of wells in those communities sits outside the local monitoring network (Bostic et al., 2023).

merced.text: Modelling against the minimum thresholds found no indication that a mitigation program would be needed. DWR required one anyway, because the interim milestones sit below historical lows (GSP §6.2.4, p. 6-12 [PDF 473]). All three GSA Boards adopted a Domestic Well Mitigation Program in early 2026 (WY 2025 Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-12 [PDF 57]). The follow-up analysis promised in the GSP, testing well impacts against those interim milestones, does not appear in the WY 2025 Annual Report. Without that analysis, a resident seeking mitigation must independently supply evidence connecting a GSA management action to their own well's failure to provide potable water (WY 2025 Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-12 [PDF 57]).

east-turlock.text: Leadership Counsel, an environmental-justice legal group, asked the GSAs to identify which domestic wells would be dewatered at the minimum thresholds. The GSAs declined, citing uncertainty over the number of currently active wells that failed in the 2015 drought (Attachment C, p. 13 of 19 [PDF 1265]). Leadership Counsel and Self-Help Enterprises produced the analysis instead, using the GSP's own published thresholds: a well counted as fully dewatered if the threshold fell below the midpoint of its screen, the intake section of the well, and partially dewatered if the threshold fell below just the top of the screen (Attachment B, Leadership Counsel letter, Figure 3 note [PDF 1159]). Of the wells they could evaluate, 5.4% came back impacted, with 3.3% fully and 2.1% partially dewatered. The GSAs did not dispute that figure; they contested the definition of a dewatered well instead, arguing some wells counted had likely already been replaced (Attachment C, p. 13 of 19 [PDF 1265]).

salinas-valley.text: The documents do not estimate domestic well exposure at the subbasin’s thresholds. The adopted action promotes DWR's statewide reporting portal (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.9, PDF p184). Over the five-year evaluation period one well was reported dry, and it lay outside SVBGSA's jurisdiction (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.9, PDF p184). Reporting is voluntary and the GSA publishes no reach figure for its promotion. The count cannot be read as an impact estimate.

kaweah.text: A Dry Well Susceptibility Analysis sized a $1.55 million minimum mitigation reserve, which is replenished each year through how allocations are set (MKGSA Mitigation Plan §5, p. 36 [PDF 44]). The analysis is not on disk, so whether it separates results by DAC status is not known. Small community wells flagged as at risk by State Water Board metrics receive proactive assistance, which may include pumping restrictions nearby (MKGSA Mitigation Plan §2.4.1 [PDF 26]). In WY 2025, eight mitigation evaluations led to three funded mitigations (Annual Report §4.4 [PDF 32]).

colusa.text: Appendix 5E counts domestic wells above candidate thresholds using state well records plus a 20-foot buffer (Appendix 5E [PDF 2714]). The revised thresholds cut projected impacts from 589 wells to 99. The GSAs estimate $3.5–6.0 million to mitigate 166 wells at thresholds and interim milestones (Appendix 5E [PDF 2711–2712]). Results are not broken down by community or DAC status.

yolo.text: The documents do not include a DAC-specific threshold or a domestic well exposure estimate. The draft well-permit review applies to proposed wells pumping more than 2 AFY, so it screens larger wells rather than domestic wells (YSGA Tiered Well Permit Review Process, draft 2024). A Domestic Well Impact Mitigation Program is listed as not yet started (GSP Appendix J, MA 7). The WY 2025 Annual Report describes work toward a possible mitigation framework (AR [PDF 10]).

sections.comparison: No basin compares protection for disadvantaged-community wells with protection elsewhere. Exposure estimates exist in Colusa (by threshold scenario), Kaweah (to size a reserve) and East Turlock (produced by advocates). Kaweah is the one basin that links the estimate to the ledger, by refilling its mitigation reserve through annual allocations.
sections.gaps: The method for thoroughly documenting well protection needs well-completion records, published thresholds and community boundaries. All six basins hold these records, and none reports the analysis by community. Colusa publishes its impacted-well definition with its threshold analysis. East Turlock’s dispute with advocates turned on that definition.

sections.title: Community Engagement
sections.literature: When examining research on ethical and equitable methods of engaging communities in water and environmental management and tool development, compensation was a major sticking point. A community asked to develop a proposal or provide input should receive the funding and technical assistance to do it (Fernandez-Bou et al., 2025). When payment wasn’t made explicitly, projects found effectiveness in substituting a delivered resource or materials taken to households (McKenna et al., 2026; Sauermilch et al., 2024). Low community turnout for participation is likely an engagement design problem (Gardner-Frolick et al., 2025).

merced.text: Translation is offered at public workshops, and workshops are sited for disadvantaged-community access (GSP §1.2.5.2, p. 1-53 [PDF 86]; GSP §3.6.1, p. 3-22 [PDF 381]). Disadvantaged-community noticing is delegated to Self-Help Enterprises and Leadership Counsel, and neither reports reach data back (GSP §1.2.5.2, p. 1-54 [PDF 87]). The bilingual materials, free technical assistance, phone line, paper application route and scored co-creation criterion all sit in the MLRP solicitation (MLRP RFP, pp. 2–3, 9, 18 [PDF 3, 17, 26]). None appears in the SGMA documents.

east-turlock.text: WY 2025 alone carried four workshops on the pumping management framework and its Proposition 218 fee assessment, five MLRP workshops, and three Stakeholder Advisory Committee meetings (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.2.2, p. 8-30 [AR PDF 73]). A grower ad hoc group also met roughly biweekly for six months while the Rules and Regulations were drafted (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.2.2, p. 8-30 [AR PDF 73]). Office hours, a help line and a GAP Help Desk ran alongside them (GSP §3.2.3, p. 3-14 [PDF 140]; WY 2025 Annual Report, p. 8-30 [AR PDF 73]). Language access is delivered through Spanish-language fact sheets, one side of a mailed bill insert, and a Spanish version of the SGMA overview video (GSP §3.5, p. 3-23 [PDF 149]). The interpreter offer is conditional: “translation to other languages can be provided when requested ahead of time” (GSP §3.5, p. 3-23 [PDF 149]). Appendix F-10 publishes per-send email open and click rates through January 2022, and none after that date is on disk (Appendix F-10, PDF 1011–1016).

salinas-valley.text: SVBGSA commissioned the Consensus Building Institute (CBI) in 2019 to conduct 14 formal interviews with community leaders on groundwater concerns and engagement barriers (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.8.1, PDF p182). The Board affirmed CBI's outreach strategy in 2021 and adopted its Spectrum of Community to Ownership as a guide, a recognized participation-ladder framework (Amendment 1 §2.7.1, PDF p60). SVBGSA adopted the spectrum as a reference tool without naming a target rung. The standing DAC advisory committee CBI recommended has not been created (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.8.1, PDF p183). Engagement instead runs through a named relationship with Castroville Community Services District. The two agencies produced joint outreach materials and shared a booth at a 2024 community resources fair (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.8.2, PDF p184). Amendment 1 commits the GSA to maintaining an active communications tracking tool (Amendment 1 §2.6.2, PDF p55), but no attendance, subscriber or response figure from it has been published in the documents reviewed.

kaweah.text: EKGSA publishes annual engagement metrics by channel, including 15 allocation email notices with over 2,000 views and four mailers to over 2,000 landowners (EKGSA Stakeholder Engagement Report [PDF 3–7]). EKGSA runs Water Dashboard help sessions twice a week during invoicing. The MKGSA Mitigation Plan commits to Spanish-language materials and at least one workshop with Spanish translation available (MKGSA Mitigation Plan §3.1.1 [PDF 32]). GKGSA documented tribal contacts through the Native American Heritage Commission (GKGSA GSP §2.7.1.9 [PDF 71]). The documents do not describe participant compensation.

colusa.text: The GSAs held 21 public meetings and workshops before October 2021, including a series of paired daytime and evening sessions (GSP §2.7.2.1 [PDF 164–167]). Flyers were produced in English and Spanish, and some meetings stayed virtual after 2021. CGA held three town halls in 2019 for named communities. Tribal participation has been limited since a tribal representative left in 2019 (GSP §2.7.3.1 [PDF 168–169]). The documents do not describe live interpretation or participant compensation.

yolo.text: The draft Communication and Engagement Plan notes that outreach during GSP development was limited by COVID-19 (GSP Appendix B [PDF 418]). The meeting log records dates and purposes without attendance. In WY 2025 the Hungry Hollow Groundwater Working Group met four times on domestic well concerns. It adopted a charter, which the YSGA Board approved (WY 2025 Annual Report [AR PDF 9]). The documents do not describe translation or participant compensation.

sections.comparison: Reach figures are published in two places: East Turlock through January 2022 and EKGSA annually. Kaweah and Yolo show engagement tied to a specific task or place, a clinic on the accounting platform and a chartered local working group. No basin compensates participants through stipends, childcare or transit.
sections.gaps: Every technique the literature recommends appears somewhere across the six basins. Compensation, which can be significantly more resource intensive, is shallower. No stipend, childcare, transit or meal provision was found in any of the six basins. The literature is also not specific about setting engagement reach targets or building them into planning and monitoring.

sections.title: Dry Well Mitigation
sections.literature: The literature establishes a widespread reality of dry well exposure and does not specifically evaluate programs. GSAs' own minimum thresholds, if reached, would dewater thousands of domestic wells, an exposure Bostic et al. (2023) estimate directly from well-construction records. Additionally, domestic wells inside disadvantaged communities are significantly less protected under those thresholds than wells outside them, a gap tied to how well a GSP integrates domestic stakeholders in planning (Perrone et al., 2023).

merced.text: All three GSA boards adopted the Domestic Well Mitigation Program in January and February 2026 (WY 2025 Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-12 [PDF 57]). It reimburses a household to a maximum of $30,000 for things like emergency water deliveries, well repair, well deepening, or connecting to alternative water supply (WY 2025 Annual Report §3.3, pp. 3-12–3-13 [PDF 57–58]). The program also treats immediate, short-term fixes with a different measure category than long-term solutions (WY 2025 Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-12 [PDF 57]). And it allows a 30-day written appeal for mitigation denial or amount awarded (WY 2025 Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-13 [PDF 58]). Funding comes from an MSGSA Proposition 218 election that capped the mitigation fund at $200,000 per year and $800,000 total (Periodic Evaluation, DWR GSP Assessment Staff Report §4.1.2.4, p. 9 of 45 [PDF 164]).

east-turlock.text: The joint Well Mitigation Plan covers impacts occurring after January 6, 2022, the GSP's adoption date (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.2.5, p. 8-33 [AR PDF 76]). It charges no fee — a full-text search of the plan returns zero occurrences of “fee” — provides a 30-day appeal with a bounded investigation (Well Mitigation Plan §3, “Appeals” [PDF 8]), and commits to multilingual flyer distribution and annual reporting (Well Mitigation Plan §5 [PDF 13]). Three dry wells were reported in WY 2025 and are being mitigated with trucked water (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.2.5, p. 8-33 [AR PDF 76]). The plan discloses 42 earlier reports — 28 from WY 2022 and 14 from WY 2023 — that remain unassessed for eligibility (Well Mitigation Plan, reproduced in WY 2025 Annual Report Appendix G [AR PDF 234]).

salinas-valley.text: A community-raised information need led to an adopted agency action. A rural well owner asked in public comment on the 2019 draft GSP — notify well owners by 2022 if groundwater levels near their well fall below the minimum threshold, so they'd have advance warning before their well actually failed (2020 GSP Appendix 11G, PDF p995). The GSA replied that this was not a requirement under SGMA (2020 GSP Appendix 11G, Response column, PDF p995). However, in 2022, Amendment 1 did adopt something addressing dry wells — Implementation Action 3 (Amendment 1, Implementation Action 3, PDF p460). The adopted action runs in the other direction: the resident reports to the agency after the well has gone dry. Promotion of DWR's existing statewide reporting tool was delivered with this action (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.9, PDF p184).

kaweah.text: The Kaweah Subbasin Mitigation Program began in 2024 and is run with Self-Help Enterprises. It commits to bottled water within 24 hours and tanks with hauled water within 72 hours (EKGSA Stakeholder Engagement Report [PDF 6]). The MKGSA plan adds a notification process to warn well owners as conditions near levels that could affect their wells. It also plans to tell existing well owners about risk when a nearby well permit is reviewed (MKGSA Mitigation Plan §2.4.2–2.4.3 [PDF 27]).

colusa.text: CGA, GGA and the Corning Subbasin GSA launched a joint Pilot Domestic Well Mitigation Program on January 1, 2026. The North Valley Community Foundation administers it (WY 2025 Annual Report §6.2.1.1, AR p. 49 [AR PDF 55]). Eligibility requires the well problem to relate to GSA management of water levels or subsidence (AR Appendix E [AR PDF 170]). Options include well deepening, consolidation and connection to public systems (GSP §6.3.7.1 [PDF 447]). No outcomes are reported yet.

yolo.text: Yolo County runs a Groundwater Assistance Program that delivers water to households with dry wells during drought emergencies. YSGA supports it with depth-to-water measurements (GSP §1.5.3.1.5 [PDF 79]). The YSGA Domestic Well Impact Mitigation Program is listed as not yet started (GSP Appendix J, MA 7).

sections.comparison: Most programs act after a household has lost water, and Kaweah plans advance notice to well owners. Eligibility in Merced, Colusa and Kaweah requires linking a well problem to groundwater conditions or management. Delivery is often contracted to a nonprofit, and Colusa’s program spans two subbasins.

sections.title: Water Quality
sections.literature: The community literature treats water quality as a translation problem rather than a measurement one. Monitoring data rewritten for a general reader has been cited in a regulatory decision (Sauermilch et al., 2024). Community-led tools earn resident trust and meet agency resistance to adoption (Pace et al., 2022; Jelks et al., 2018). No reviewed paper addresses which constituents a groundwater agency should track.

merced.text: Drinking water protection was raised as a priority by beneficial users to the GSA (GSP §3.6.1, p. 3-22 [PDF 381]). The technical scope was set separately, in consultation with the county Division of Environmental Health. The GSAs determined that “salinity is the only constituent of concern currently known to be directly tied to groundwater management activities” (GSP §3.6.1, p. 3-22 [PDF 381]). Nitrate therefore sits outside the criteria.

east-turlock.text: Six constituents of concern carry the water quality thresholds, set at their maximum contaminant levels (Attachment C, pp. 12–17 of 19 [PDF 1264–1269]). The network includes 160 domestic wells, most sampled for nitrate alone (Attachment C, p. 17 of 19 [PDF 1269]). Requests to add manganese, hexavalent chromium and PFAS were declined, largely because standards or data do not yet exist (Attachment C, pp. 12 and 16 of 19 [PDF 1264, 1268]). Expanded domestic well testing runs through the State Water Board's SAFER program rather than the GSA (Attachment C, p. 17 of 19 [PDF 1269]).

salinas-valley.text: Amendment 1 tabulates roughly twenty constituents with exceedance counts drawn from state monitoring data (Amendment 1 §5.4.1, Table 5-6, PDF p185). Thresholds reference Title 22 drinking water standards for public system and on-farm domestic wells, and Basin Plan objectives for irrigation wells (Amendment 1 §5.4.1, PDF p185). On-farm domestic wells sit inside the Irrigated Lands network (Amendment 1 §5.4.1, PDF p185). One of Castroville's four supply wells went offline in 2021 on chloride from seawater intrusion (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.8.2, PDF p183).

kaweah.text: Since 2025 the three GSAs sample an expanded list of constituents each spring and fall at 75 sites (Groundwater Quality Report, Spring 2026 [PDF 2]). Site selection was prioritized in or near disadvantaged communities (GKGSA GSP App. 3B [PDF 2305–2318]). A plain-language seasonal report points residents to free well testing and invites them to share their results (Groundwater Quality Report [PDF 5]). The report describes itself as an interim step until enough wells are registered to support direct alerts.

colusa.text: Electrical conductivity is the one constituent with a minimum threshold (WY 2025 Annual Report Table 6-3). The network includes one well from each community public water system, 11 in total (GSP §4.2.5.2, p. 4-37 [PDF 326]). Nitrate and arsenic are described in the basin setting. The documents do not describe a community-facing water quality product.

yolo.text: TDS carries the minimum threshold (1,000 ppm) and measurable objective (750 ppm), added in response to a public comment (GSP comment matrix [PDF 460]). Nitrate, arsenic and hexavalent chromium are discussed in the GSP. Yolo County provides nitrate fact sheets to well owners in English and Spanish (GSP comment matrix [PDF 463]).

sections.comparison: Threshold coverage ranges from one constituent (Merced, Colusa, Yolo) to about twenty (Salinas Valley). Thresholds in every basin reference adopted standards. Kaweah is the one basin with a community-facing water quality report, and it invites residents to share their own test results.

sections.title: Domestic Wells and Community Water System Consolidation
sections.literature: The missing dataset in this area is a trust problem rather than a technical one. Statewide service-area boundaries for small water systems sat largely incomplete for a decade. They reached near-completion only once the work shifted to relationship-building with the staff holding the local knowledge (McDonald et al., 2026). Wells inside disadvantaged communities are the least documented of any group (Bostic et al., 2023).

merced.text: MIUGSA’s Domestic Well Inventory and Outreach project hired Self-Help Enterprises to contact landowners and improve well location, construction and performance records. Over roughly three years and about $125,000 it improved information on approximately 30 wells (PE §8.1, p. 8-5 [PDF 134]). Machine-parsing the state’s well completion reports located roughly 400 in the same period (PE §8.1, p. 8-5 [PDF 134]). The GSP reproduces a county policy encouraging consolidation of single-user wells into water districts (GSP p. 1-41 [PDF 74]).

east-turlock.text: The East Turlock documents do not describe a domestic well inventory. The richest dataset bearing on the subbasin was assembled by Leadership Counsel and Self-Help Enterprises from public sources (Attachment B, Leadership Counsel letter [PDF 1159]). The fee regime exempts de minimis extractors and charges small community water systems. Their allocation is computed from the “acreage of the service area” of the system (Rules and Regulations Phase 2 §5.01).

salinas-valley.text: The Community Water Center described a regional mapping tool showing disadvantaged communities, contamination areas and nearby water district boundaries, built partly to evaluate consolidation options for small communities (2020 GSP Appendix 11G, PDF p1124). It is named in a comment letter and not adopted in the plan. County policies reproduced in the GSP encourage consolidation and prefer connection to public utilities (2020 GSP §3.10, p. 3-31 [PDF p85]). The Salinas Valley documents do not describe a domestic well inventory.

kaweah.text: A phased, voluntary Well Registration Program was scheduled to open to all well owners in Spring 2026 (MKGSA Mitigation Plan §2.4.4 [PDF 27–28]). The plan anticipates some hesitation from owners concerned about privacy and property values. The same registry is named as the input for ISW depletion estimates, at-risk well notices and water quality alerts. The mitigation claims checklist includes a step to investigate consolidation feasibility (MKGSA GSP App. 6D [PDF 3778]).

colusa.text: Domestic well data comes from DWR’s well completion reports. About half lack screen-depth information, and many locations are mapped to section centroids (Appendix 5E [PDF 2714]). Well inventory and well registration programs are listed as GSP Studies (GSP §7.1.2.8–7.1.2.9 [PDF 518–519]). Consolidation is one of six mitigation options for individual households (GSP §6.3.7.1 [PDF 447]).

yolo.text: A USBR WaterSMART grant funds a domestic well inventory. Staff and consultants used an AI-assisted method to geolocate well completion reports, and the work was nearly complete at the end of WY 2025 (WY 2025 Annual Report [AR PDF 10]). The documents do not describe community water system consolidation.

sections.comparison: Domestic well data in every basin traces to state well completion records. Three basins are improving them: Merced through outreach, Yolo through automated geolocation, and Kaweah through voluntary registration. Consolidation appears as county policy or as a household mitigation option (Colusa, Kaweah). It is not a groundwater accounting action in any basin.

sections.title: Data and Decision-Support Integration
sections.literature: The literature offers a method for deciding what a tool should contain. It works back from a named decision to the data that decision requires (Cantor et al., 2021; Jelks et al., 2018). Adding community-reported information measurably improved a technical model in one test (Gardner-Frolick et al., 2025). Timeliness and ownership are the reported failure points (McKenna et al., 2026; Pace et al., 2022).

merced.text: The Groundwater Accounting Platform is the mandatory compliance channel under the July 2026 Rules (WY 2025 Annual Report §3.3, p. 3-10 [PDF 55]; MSGSA Rules and Regulations, July 2026), and everything is filed through it in English. The named external tools in use are the SGMA Data Viewer, the Water Data Library, GAMA and the DAC Mapping Tool, all agency-facing (WY 2025 Annual Report §3.4, p. 3-14 [AR PDF 59]; AR p. 2-30 [PDF 45]; GSP §1.2.2.2.1.1, p. 1-29 [PDF 62]; GSP p. 1-51 [PDF 84]). MercedMAR is described as a decision-support tool listing drinking water users and domestic well owners among its intended users. No community-facing view of the platform is described.

east-turlock.text: The Annual Report describes the accounting platform as grower-facing (WY 2025 Annual Report §8.2.5, p. 8-36 [AR PDF 79]), and the GSP's engagement chapter contains no occurrence of its name (GSP Chapter 3, full-text search). The tools in use are the SGMA Data Viewer, the Water Data Library and DWR's dry well reporting portal (WY 2025 Annual Report §2, p. 2-1 [AR PDF 17]; GSP p. 2-12 [PDF 78]; WY 2025 Annual Report §8.1.1.4, p. 8-14 [AR PDF 57]). The subbasin holds two unjoined assets. A door-to-door community survey feeds repurposing planning (MLRP Outreach & Engagement Plan, p. 4 [OCR PDF 4]), and a 400-metre sensitive-receptor buffer turned a health concern into a mapped layer (Technical Memorandum §1.5, p. 12 [PDF 12]).

salinas-valley.text: SVBGSA maintains a data management system and a public web map (Periodic Evaluation §7.4.9, PDF p184; 2020 GSP ES-6, PDF p32). Amendment 1 describes mailings targeted at the most-impacted water users, delivered with the tax bill and including an Annual Report dashboard (Amendment 1 §2.6.6, PDF p57). The WY 2025 Annual Report records a completed story map, subbasin one-pagers in preparation and an activated website translation feature (WY 2025 Annual Report, Table 4-1, p. 68 [AR PDF 75]). The documents do not report use figures for these products.

kaweah.text: The Water Dashboard is the landowner-facing accounting platform, showing allocations, monthly ET use and a trading module (MKGSA GSP §6.7.1.1 [PDF 389]). Community-facing products are separate: the Groundwater Quality Report and an EKGSA Projects webpage with an interactive map (EKGSA Stakeholder Engagement Report [PDF 8]). SAFER is the one named state tool pointed at residents.

colusa.text: Public information is shared as documents: websites, newsletters, flyers and the Annual Report. The one data tool the GSAs point the public to is OpenET (GSP §2.7.3.6 [PDF 170]). In late 2025 the GSAs selected a consultant team to build a subbasin water accounting system (WY 2025 Annual Report §6.2.1.2, AR p. 50 [AR PDF 56]). The documents do not describe a community-facing component for it.

yolo.text: The DWR DAC Mapping Tool and SGMA Data Viewer are used as data sources and reach the public as static figures (GSP §1.5.2 [PDF 64]). Community comments led to new DAC, tribal lands and well depth layers in the GSP. The documents do not describe a tool that returns data to residents.

sections.comparison: Kaweah runs a landowner accounting platform alongside separate public products, the two-tier setup the GAP community use case describes. Merced and East Turlock run a platform without a public layer. Salinas Valley has public products without a platform, and Colusa is procuring its platform now. No GSA in the six basins uses CalEnviroScreen.
sections.gaps: No basin has worked back from a community decision to the data it would need. None has tested whether community-reported information would improve a model it already maintains. The reviewed tool cases were built for communities from the start, so none addresses a compliance platform with a separate community audience.

chapters.closing_note: The six document sets are not equally complete. Merced's three GSAs share one GSP and differ on procedural access. The standing disadvantaged-community seat is MIUGSA's and the fee-gated appeals are MSGSA's. TIWD GSA-1 has no instrument on disk. In the Turlock Subbasin the Rules, the fee, the accounting platform and the MLRP outreach contract are East Turlock's. In Salinas Valley all community material reviewed is SVBGSA's. Merced and East Turlock each have a binding accounting rulebook against which equity provisions can be tested, and Salinas Valley has none. East Turlock's GSP appendices carry a comment response matrix, a stakeholder gap analysis, published email metrics and two surveys (Appendix F-15 [PDF 1252–1271]; Appendix F-2 [PDF 962–967]; Appendix F-10 [PDF 1011–1016]; Appendix F-13 [PDF 1029–1039]). Merced has no counterpart to any of them and received no comments on its 2025 plan (GSP §1.2.5.6, p. 1-57 [PDF 90]), so several comparisons here rest on two basins. Much of Salinas Valley’s community material was written by commenters. Kaweah’s three GSAs file separate GSPs, and MKGSA has no rulebook on disk, so its findings come from its GSP and Mitigation Plan. The Kaweah engagement metrics are EKGSA’s only. Colusa has no rules-and-regulations instrument; its GSP and two MOUs are its governing instruments, and its JPA agreements are not on disk. Yolo’s most current community content appears in the WY 2025 Annual Report narrative. Neither Colusa nor Yolo has a Periodic Evaluation on disk.
